                                                                                 FM 7-73 —

                                                              CHAPTER 5

                                              Offense
Offense is the means by which the attacker carries the battle to the enemy and
destroys his will to fight, and the BFV gives the infantry a potent offensive
weapon. The BF'V has a weapons system — the 25-mm gun — that is primarily
designed to kill BMPs beyond 2,000 meters. In addition, the BF'V can kill tanks
with its TOW at 3,750 meters and nonarmored vehicles and unprotected enemy
personnel at 900 meters with its 7.62-mm coaxial-mounted machine gun.

                                         Section !. Capabilities

To add to the vehicle’s tremendous firepower,the BF'V can shoot on the
move, shoot at night, keep up with the M1 tank, and protect its
occupants from artillery fragments and machine gun fire up to

14.5-mm (.58 caliber).

    —FM 7-73    5.1. Employment.
5-2
                as The BF'V’s capabilities allow mechanized infantry with the BFV
                        to be employed offensively:

                        (1) From long overwatch positions (1 ,000-3,000 meters) that
                                 allow the BF'V to suppress enemy BMPs, tanks, and ATGMs
                                  at a relatively safe standoff distance.

                        (2) Suppressing on the move when supporting tanks by following
                                 and protecting their flanks and rear from ATGMs, and
                                 dismounting infantry when necessary to clear obstacles,
                                 ATGMs, enemy dismounted infantry, and maintain the
                                   momentum of the tanks.

                       (3) By separating the BFVs from the infantry and fighting each
                                in such a way as to maximize the capabilities of both
                                (dismounted infantry using restrictive terrain to assault the
                                objective, while vehicles support from long overwatch).

                       (4) With dismounted infantry in close overwatch (0-500 meters)
                                while tanks and BFVs assault an objective.

                      Despite its increased capabilities, however, the BFV has some
                      limitations that must be considered in its employment. The BFV is
                       not a light tank. Though it is quick and agile with an impressive
                       array of weapons, it does not have the armor protection to allow it
                       to travel around the battlefield like a tank. It must use covered and
                       concealed routes when possible as well as hull-down firing
                      positions. It cannot move across open ground against an
                      entrenched and prepared enemy, or it will be destroyed.

              5-2. Basic tactics.

              a. Platoons and squads normally conduct offensive operations as
                      part of a company or company team. In a company team,
                     mechanized infantry platoons and squads operate in conjunction
                     with one or more armor platoons. Usually the company team
                      commander specifies a combination of tank and infantry to be
                     used during an operation. For example in a deliberate attack, he
                     may direct that tanks lead across the LD, dismounted infantry
                     lead through a small forest, tanks lead to dismount point,
                     dismounted infantry moves forward on a covered and concealed
                     route and supports a tank assault from close overwatch, and BFVs
                     support from long overwatch.

—FM 7-73   Because a BF'V will seldom move and fight alone on the battlefield,
5-4        the tactical focus of Bradley mechanized infantry is at platoon
           level. Platoons employ drills and tactics; squads execute drills.
           Employment of the BFV platoon is complicated by the requirement
           to control two distinct elements: the dismounted troops and the
           vehicles. Unlike earlier infantry carriers, the BFV element can
           fight in conjunction with or separated from the dismounted
           element. This means that although the BFV and its crew fight as
           one system when mounted, they fight as two separate systems
           when the rifle team dismounts and moves off on its own mission
           under the control of the platoon leader. For the squad leader, at the
           moment of dismount, a change occurs in the control of the squad.
          Since the squad leader cannot usually control both the rifle team
           and the vehicle, once separated, he gives control of one or the other
          to the assistant squad leader. If he stays with the vehicle, he gives
           control of the rifle team to the platoon’s dismount element leader,
          usually the platoon leader. If the squad leader dismounts, he gives
          control of the vehicle to the platoon’s vehicle element leader,
          usually the platoon sergeant.

          Because platoons and squads normally conduct offensive
          operations as part of a company or company team, their offensive
          tasks are part of a movement to contact and subsequent hasty
          attack mission, or as part of a deliberate attack mission. The type
          of operation the company team will conduct is dictated by the
          mission.

          Another major factor that influences the type of operation is how
          much resistance the unit expects to encounter. The nature of the
          resistance is a critical part of the “E” in METT-T and as such
          influences the actions of leaders and options available to them.

          (1) Light resistance. Enemy squad or platoon-size element
                   defending on the best available terrain feature without
                   combined arms (engineer, artillery) assets. Normally, the
                   force will be made up of two to three vehicles of the same type
                   (BRDM, BMP or tank pure), some AT assets, and positions
                   will not be dug in. The force will usually attempt to hold its
                  position since its mission includes maintaining contact and
                   reporting on our location and disposition.

          (2) Medium resistance. Enemy of platoon or company-size
                   with individual fighting positions, but not well prepared. The
                   enemy position will be organized around the best defensible
                   terrain with combined arms assets integrated.

          (3) Heavy resistance. Enemy will have established platoon
                   and company strongpoints. Defense will be echeloned and


---

                                                                        FM 7-73 —

        extensive minefields, tank ditches, and wire obstacles will be
        in place. The defense will have integrated all arms, and heavy
        artillery fire can be expected. The enemy will have platoon
        size elements in the security zone forward of the main
        defensive belt. Units generally will not withdraw or move to
        alternate positions once the main defensive belt is attacked.

The company team commander plans for his offensive mission
based on the mission given to him by his task force commander as
well as his own estimate of the situation. His estimate is based (toa
large extent) on his analysis of METT-T, and results in one of three
types of missions — movement to contact, hasty attack, or
deliberate attack. The primary difference between a hasty and
deliberate attack is the planning and coordination time available
to the commander or leader that allows him to integrate all of the
combined arms assets (CAS, indirect fires, EW, smoke, engineer)
into his attack plan. Often, a hasty attack occurs as a result of
chance or unexpected contact or when the commander chooses to
attack quickly before the enemy can use the additional time for his

own advantage.

A company team commander may be given either a movement to
contact, hasty attack, or deliberate attack mission based on a
number of tactical factors.

. Thedeliberate attack occurs when more time is available for
     planning and coordination and enemy resistance is expected to be
     heavy. Reconnaissance is used to get as much information on
     enemy strength and location as possible. All elements of the
     combined arms team are carefully integrated (BFVs, tanks,
     artillery, helicopters, CAS) into the plan for attack. The possibility
     for conducting a night attack is considered.

— FM 7-73

                                               Section Il. Movement to Contact

           Generally, when a unit is moving toward but not in contact with the
           enemy, it is conducting a movement to contact. Many offensive
           operations begin with a movement to contact. Its purpose is to gain or
           regain enemy contact and to develop the situation to conduct an attack.
           Movement to contact is usually characterized by limited information
           about the enemy.

           5-3. Missions.

           a. Platoons and squads participate in a movement to contact as part
                  of the company or company team using the movement techniques
                  explained in Chapter 4. The lead platoon in the movement to
                  contact has several critical tasks to perform. These missions are:

                   (1) Protecting the company or company team from a surprise
                           attack by providing early warning of enemy positions and
                            obstacles.

                  (2) Assisting the forward movement of the company or company
                           team by removing obstacles or finding routes around them.

                  (3) Defeating enemy forces within the platoon’s ability.
                  (4) Developing the situation rapidly once contact is made by

                           assessing the situation and sending a spot report to the team
                           commander.

                  The remaining platoons within the company or company team are
                  assigned missions and positions within the formation based on
                  the movement techniques being used. Their missions normally
                  include overwatching the lead platoon and reacting with fire
                  and/or movement once contact is made.

           5-4. Planning.

           a. A platoon normally moves as part of a company team along an
                  axis of advance. An axis of advance provides the platoon leader
                  flexibility to move his BFVs as necessary to bypass obstacles or
                  impassable terrain. The axis also allows the platoon to move
                  according to the commander’s intent. The exact route selected by
                  the platoon leader must keep the platoon oriented and allow the
                  company or company team to move with minimum difÏculty.

                  Because the platoon leader does not know when or where he will
                  make contact with the enemy, he should avoid mounted movement


---

on terrain such as draws, ravines, narrow trails, or steep slopes         FM 7-7J —
that restricts movement. In addition, the platoon leader must also                      5-13
consider the speed at which the commander expects him to
advance and select his route accordingly.

A line of departure, phase lines, and checkpoints are normally
assigned to control and coordinate the forward movement of the
company or company team. The platoon leader may be required to
report the crossing of phase lines to the company or company team
commander, but the platoon does not stop at a phase line unless
told to do so. If necessary, the platoon leader may designate
additional phase lines or checkpoints for internal platoon use to
reduce the number and length of orders to control movement.

Fire control and distribution is accomplished through the use of
boundaries, fire plans, pyrotechnics, and weapons-ready posture.
It takes on added importance in the movement to contact because
of the scarcity of information about the enemy. The weapons-ready
posture must not only be flexible enough to respond to an unclear
enemy situation but also varies between the bounding and
overwatching elements. It is critical in BFV units because of the
variety of weapons that can be controlled from the turret and
dangers of expending all of the on-board ammunition of a weapon

within the platoon.

 (1) Theoverwatching element should consider erecting their
       TOWs and performing the self-test although not all will be
        designated to fire. The platoon leader should also designate
        which vehicles will prepare 25-mm HEI-T, APDS, and

          7.62-mm coax.

 (2) Ifrestrictive terrain dominates the route, the bounding
        element may not have the same fields of fire as the overwatching
        element and may be less capable of employing its TOWs.
        Once again, the leader should designate which vehicles will
        be prepared to fire the various weapons and types of

          ammunition.

Fire planning is crucial in the movement to contact because the
enemy situation is often poorly defined and the place where
contact will occur is unknown. The FO is the principal assistant to
the platoon leader in fire planning. Platoon leaders should plan
fires along the entire route, specifically at possible contact points
 (key terrain, choke points) and on identifiable terrain features to

 aid in shifting fires.


---

—FM 7-7J          The platoon leader must ensure that his FO coordinates and
 5-14             updates the fire plan with the FSO at company team level. If this is
                 not done, a platoon leader who makes contact may not utilize all
                  the fires that the company team has made available to him.

                 Air guards are especially critical in a movement to contact. If the
                 cargo hatch is open, an air guard can be designated to watch to the
                 sides and rear — front view is blocked by turret. The Bradley
                 commander in one or more of the BFVs will have to act as an air
                 guard oriented to the front.

                 Once contact is made with the enemy, the platoon should not break
                 contact unless ordered to by the company commander.Additionally,
                 the platoon leader should develop the situation by gathering and
                 reporting critical information about the enemy and recommending
                 a course of action.

          5-5. Actions on Contact.

          Whena platoon makes contact, it must react quickly and aggressively
          using battle drills. The platoon’s actions in the first few seconds after
          contact may determine whether a battle is won or lost. Those actions
          must include several initial moves that occur almost simultaneously:
          return fire, deploy, report. The platoon leader must then:

          a. Develop the situation. The platoon leader should act quickly to
                 determine the enemy’s strength, composition, and disposition. He
                  may call for indirect fire support and use fire and movement to
                 develop the situation. In doing so, he should attempt to overrun the
                 position if enemy resistance is weak. He should not expose his
                 BFVs needlessly. The rifle teams normally remain mounted so the
                 platoon can move without delay. The degree of resistance and type
                 of enemy fire influence the platoon leader’s recommendation to the
                 company or company team commander on a course of action to be
                 taken.

                 Choose a course of action. Based on his observation of the
                 enemy, the platoon leader can recommend several actions if the
                 enemy force cannot be overrun.

                 (1) Bypass. If the enemy does not present a meaningful threat
                          and bypass routes are available, the platoon leader does not
                          allow light enemy resistance to slow forward movement
                          unless it poses a threat to the rest of the company team.

                 (2) Conducta hasty attack. If the enemy resistance is light, he
                          can recommend a hasty attack to destroy the enemy force. He


---

                                                                           FM 7-7J —

           normally does not attack unless the team commander
           approves, but may choose to overrun very light resistance if
            his mission orders indicate so.

    (3) Fix and suppress. If there is strong enemy resistance and
           the platoon cannot move, the platoon leader can have the
           platoon’s fires fix and suppress the enemy. This is done using
           direct and indirect fires to hold the enemy in position while
           the rest of the company or company team moves to conduct a
           hasty attack, uses engineers to breach obstacles, or bypasses.
           To fix the enemy, the platoon leader deploys his vehicles and
           possibly his infantry and assumes an overwatch position to
           take the enemy under fire and limit the enemy’s ability to

                 maneuver.

    Report. As soon as the platoon leader has reached a protected
    position, he should pass to the company commander all he knows
    about the enemy. Once the platoon leader has developed the
    situation and decided on a course of action, he updates his earlier
    report to the commander. In some cases, the commander may

    change the platoon leader’s plan.

— FM 7-7J                                             Section Ill. Hasty Attack
5-16
           Attacks are conducted to destroy or capture an enemy force and to
           secure key terrain. An attack can be either hasty or deliberate. The
           basic difference between these two types of attacks is dictated by the
           amount of time available for detailed planning and preparation. Hasty
           attacks are more common in movement to contact situations and are
           executed quickly using squad and platoon drills.

           5-6. Options.

           When contact is made and the decision is to conduct a hasty attack, the
           platoon leader has two options. He can attack mounted or dismounted.
           In most cases, the decision as to whether or not to dismount will be
           made after informing the company team commander of the situation
           and with his approval, although in some quickly developing situations
           the platoon leader may make the dismount decision himself.

           a. When to attack mounted.

                   (1) Because the BFV is not heavily armored, the decision to
                           remain mounted for the hasty attack is a critical one. The key
                            considerations governing the decision whether or not to
                           remain mounted are:

                            (a) Orders from the company team commander.

                           (b) Degree of enemy resistance (light).

                            (c) TrafÏcability (good without too much open exposure).

                  (2) If tanks are also participating in the hasty attack, they will
                           normally lead and the BFVs will follow 200 to 400 meters to
                           their rear suppressing known or suspected enemy ATGM
                            positions and protecting the tanks from dismounted enemy
                           AT teams. They will dismount only if the tanks to their front
                           require an area to be cleared or if an ATGM position to the
                           flank must be reduced to maintain the momentum of the
                           attack. Some degree of risk must always be accepted when
                           attacking mounted.

                  (3) Iftanks cannot lead because of the enemy threat, then it will
                           not be prudent to attack mounted with BFVs either.

                  (4) The decision to attack mounted without tanks should only
                           occur with a BFV pure force against extremely light
                           resistance or when terrain precludes attacking with tanks.

                  (5) Once the decision is made to conduct a mounted hasty attack,
                          the Bradley platoon leader must still be prepared to dismount
                           if resistance stiffens, trafÏcability turns out to be poorer than


---

         anticipated, or an unexpected threat emerges that can best be     FM 7-73 —
         dealt with by dismounted infantry.                                             5-17

When to attack dismounted.

(1) The decision to conduct a dismounted hasty attack is critical
         because it is inherently slower than attacking mounted and
         might give the enemy time to stiffen his defenses. Additionally,
        it might cause the momentum of the movement-to-contact
         operation to be lost. The key considerations governing the
         decision whether or not to dismount are:

         (a) Orders from the company team commander.

         (b) Degree of enemy resistance known or expected
                  (medium).

         (c) Amount of restrictive terrain.

         (d) Significant ATGM threat.

(2) As the degree of enemy resistance increases and especially as

        the ATGM threat increases, the ability to attack mounted
        decreases. Tanks are capable of maneuvering against
        medium resistance because of their armor protection, but
         BF'Vs will primarily conduct long overwatch support for the
        dismounted element in those situations.

(3) The sameis true with restrictive terrain. Forests, ravines, and

        built-up areas are ideal locations for enemy ATGM, both
        mounted and dismounted. Dismounted infantry should be
        used to conduct the hasty attack unless intelligence indicates
        that the enemy has little or no AT capability — an unusual
        situation.

(4) The selection of a dismount point requires that leaders make

        a map reconnaissance before the operation, and monitor the
        terrain as the unit passes through it. This is especially
        important as the unit approaches and passes through close
        terrain. If the platoon is required to dismount, the vehicles
        should move to a dismount point:

         (a) That is as far forward as possible.

        (b) Where vehicles can be close enough to one another to
                  facilitate forming the platoon.

         (c) Where vehicles are out of the direct fire line and indirect
                 fire impact area.

        (d) Where vehicles have some cover or concealment.

                    dismount. It usually occurs when the unit takes effective fire
                    and cannot proceed without having the enemy cleared. To
                    conduct a hasty dismount, the platoon leader:

                    (a) Receives orders or makes the decision himself to
                             dismount.

                    (b) Quickly scans the area to select a likely dismount point.

                    (c) Directs his driver and his platoon sergeant to move

                    (d) Alerts the rifle teams to prepare for dismount.

                    (e) Occupies the hasty dismount point, forming the platoon

                    (f) Verifies that the dismount point is suitable.

                    (g) Orders the dismount and forms the platoon.

                    (h) Leaves instructions with the platoon sergeant (vehicle

                             an overwatch position where they can support by fire).

                    (i) Issues a hasty FRAGO to the dismounted platoon and

                                moves out.

           (6) Once the infantry has dismounted, the BFVs move to an

                    overwatch position where they can support by fire. In cases
                   where long overwatch is possible, the BFVs move farther to
                   the rear to take advantage of their standoff ranges. In other
                   cases, the terrain may require that they overwatch from a
                   closer position.

           Overwatch.

           (1) When the company or company team is using bounding

                    overwatch, the overwatch force (normally at least one pla-
                    toon) must be ready, once contact is made, to suppress enemy
                    weapons that endanger the bounding force.

           (2) When a Bradley commander or gunner in an overwatch

                    position spots an antitank gun or ATGM fired, or in position
                   to fire, he immediately opens fire with the 25-mm gun (using
                    HEI-T) on the weapon’s position, or he fires at the base of the
                    smoke trail or at the gun flash, and gives the warning over the
                    radio.

           (3) When the company or company team is using traveling

                   overwatch, the overwatch platoon quickly fires on the enemy
                   from covered firing positions. It avoids moving into areas

                                                                            FM 7-7J —

            where it may be caught by enemy fire directed at the lead
            platoon or fire that prevents it from moving toward the
            enemy. The platoon remains mounted to reduce vulnerability
            to enemy indirect fire and to allow it to move quickly. The
            platoon continues enemy suppression until the lead platoon
            reaches covered positions. The overwatch platoon then
            engages only clearly identified targets or areas designated by
            the company or company team commander.

-7. Maneuver.

Aaneuver is the movement of forces supported by fire to achieve a
osition of advantage over the enemy. It consists of two actions that
ake place at the same time. The base-of-fire element covers a moving
orce by firing at the enemy position and by employing indirect fires.
‘he moving force moves forward to close with the enemy or to reach a
etter position from which to fire at the enemy. Depending on the
istance to the enemy position and the amount of cover and
oncealment available, the base-of-fire element and the moving force
nay switch roles as needed to continue maneuvering. Before the
noving force advances beyond the supporting range of the base-of-fire
lement, it takes a position from which it can fire on the enemy, and the
ase-of-fire element becomes the moving force.

                 (1) The company commander may have one platoon support by

                           The support-by-fire platoon occupies dominating positions

                (2) The support-by-fire platoon will suppress known or expected

                          enemy positions two to three kilometers away. Their main
                          task is to provide fire to keep the enemy’s head down, to kill
                          dismounted infantry and thin-skinned vehicles, and to
                          destroy antitank weapons systems. To suppress enemy

                          dismounted personnel.

                          move under fire, the fighting vehicles generally work in pairs
                          using the wingman concept. Two vehicles (one pair) support
                          by fire, while the other two move. The wingman generally
                           follows to the flank and rear of his leader (platoon leader or
                          platoon sergeant) and provides security for that leader while
                          also engaging targets of opportunity that are acquired while
                          on the move.

                (4) When the commander travels with the moving platoons, the

                            company executive ofÏcer (2IC) may be positioned with the
                           support-by-fire platoon to coordinate the employment of
                           direct and indirect fires to fit the scheme of maneuver
                          established in the operation order.

          b. Dismounted.

                (1) How members of a rifle team move depends on the intensity of

                          enemy fire. Crawling may be called for when a moving
                          dismount element faces intense fire and there is little cover.
                          Soldiers use the low or high crawl depending on the situation,
                          the requirement for speed, and the example of their leader.
                          Progress is slow here, but exposure to enemy observation and
                          fire is reduced. When not moving forward, the individual
                          infantryman delivers suppressive fire on the enemy. If
                          necessary, infantrymen may advance all the way into and
                          through positions by crawling.

                (2) Short rushes from covered position to covered position may

                          be used when enemy fire allows brief exposure. Rifle teams,
                          two-man teams, or individuals may advance by short rushes
                          to avoid accurate enemy fire. Soldiers should not stay up

8. Techniques of fire.

   The base-of-fire element uses its fire to cover and protect the
   advance of the moving force. Whenever possible, the base-of-fire
   element should move undetected into a firing position. A high
   volume of surprise fire has a greater effect than fire delivered from
   a known position.

   When the base-of-fire element is in position, the following usually
   takes place:

   (1) A heavy volume of fire is placed on the enemy position to
           destroy or suppress it.

   (2) When the enemy position is suppressed, the rate of fire is
           reduced. However, suppression continues.

   (3) When the moving force nears its objective, the rate of fire is
            increased to keep the enemy down. This lets the moving force
           assault the position before the enemy can react.

Effective fire on the enemy is the key to forward movement. Fires
are directed at destroying or suppressing the enemy. Suppressive
fire is placed on the enemy to keep him from firing effectively at the
moving force.

The base-of-fire element can concentrate or distribute its fire. In
either case, the fire must be controlled. The fire must be effectively
directed at the enemy and not endanger the moving force.

There are two types of fire that the base-of-fire element can deliver
in support of the moving force.

(1) Point fire. Point fire is directed against a specific identified
         target, such as a machine gun or ATGM position. All
         weapons are fired at the target. Spreading out the base-of-fire
        element fires aids in point fire because the fire is directed from
         multiple directions. Point fire is not often used, since the
         platoon seldom encounters a single, clearly identified enemy

              weapon.

(2) Area fire. Area fire is distributed over a larger area when
        enemy positions are more numerous or less obvious. Each
        weapon or BF'V in the base-of-fire element is given a specific
        sector of the target area to fire into. This is done to ensure that
        the entire target area is covered by fire and observation.

            5-9. Assault techniques.

            If destruction of the enemy is required, it may be done either by fire or
            close assault. Destruction by fire is preferred because it takes
            advantage of the BFV’s weapons systems and their long standoff
            ranges. Destruction by fire limits the exposure of dismounted
            personnel to the enemy’s fires and allows the platoon leader to better
            protect and conserve his dismounted infantry.

            If destruction cannot be accomplished by fire, an assault of the enemy
            position may be required. If the enemy resistance is light or medium, an

     Assaulting mounted.

    (1) When resistance includes little or no antitank defenses, the

             platoon may be directed to attack mounted. If tanks are
              available, the assault is capable of overcoming heavier
              resistance. If tanks are not available, amounted assault
              should be attempted only against light resistance.

    (2) The mounted assault should be done with tanks leading and

              BF'Vs supporting on the move. The BFVs should orient their
              turret weapons on ATGM and dismounted targets that could
              slow the tanks. Firing port weapons should be manned to
              ensure a high volume of suppressive firing during the assault.
              As the BFVs assault over the objective, care must be taken to
              ensure the bypassed enemy infantry are not able to emerge
              from their trenches and attack the tanks and BFVs with close
              range AT weapons.

    (3) The assault should be coordinated with suppressive indirect

              fire, especially VT, that would not pose a threat to the tanks
              and BFVs.

    (4) A tentative dismount point should be selected if the enemy

             begins to place effective AT fires on the unit.

    Assaulting dismounted. When assaulting dismounted, the
    infantry platoon has three options:

    (1) With tanks. The assaulting infantry breaches the obstacle

             line while tanks provide close support to suppress the enemy.
             The BFVs provide long overwatch and aid in the suppression
             effort. Once the breach is accomplished, the tanks are passed
             through and overrun the objective. The infantry follow
             quickly to clear the trench linde and ensure that the enemy is
             not able to attack the tanks at close range.

    (2) Separate from tanks. Dismounted infantry movestoa

             position where it can provide close overwatch for the tank
             assault. Theinfantry may attack the enemy by fire only from
             a flank or the rear or may assault to divert attention from the
             tank assault and unhinge the enemy defense. The BFVs
              provide long overwatch to suppress the enemy and destroy
             point targets of opportunity.

          Actions of the dismount element.

          (1) If an assault position has been designated, the dismount

                  element uses it to deploy. As little time as possible is spent in
                  the assault position and the deployment into the assault
                  formation should be made as rapidly as possible.

          (2) When the rifle teams are generally on line, the platoon leader
                  moves them forward using fire and movement. The final
                  assault is not a stand-up, on-line rush. In the assault, squad
                  leaders lead by example because it is hard for oral orders to be
                  understood. “Follow me and do as I do” is the way to lead.

          (3) Squad leaders must lead on through the enemy positions.

                  They move using the best method for the situation. The
                  soldiers follow that example. The advance may be by
                  crawling or by short rushes from cover position to cover
                  position. It must be aggressively done because the dismount
                  element cannot stop once it is near the enemy. As it fights its
                  way through the objective (still using fire and movement), the
                  dismount element must avoid exposing itself to fire from
                   enemy forces behind or to the flanks of the objective. Soldiers
                   must not bunch up and make good targets.

          (4) Normally, the entire dismount element moves forward to

                  assault the enemy, supported by BF'Vs, tanks, and ITVs.
                  When their fire is not adequate to support the assault, the
                   platoon leader may set up his own base of fire.

                  the objective, actions by squad leaders are the key to fire
                   distribution. Squad leaders move near the center of their team
                   where their own men can see them. Most of the time, they
                   control fire by firing their own weapon into the area where
                   they want their men to fire. They also can use arm-and-hand
                   signals. At times, short, easily understood oral orders can be
                   used, but in many cases oral orders will be drowned out by
                  battle noises.

                                                  Section IV. Deliberate Attack

           The deliberate attack is one in which ample time is available for
            planning and coordination. It is often necessary when enemy
           resistance is medium to heavy and the enemy’s defensive line must be
           breached. To ensure success and preclude heavy casualties, a careful
           integration of tanks, infantry, artillery, mortars, engineers, and other
           combat support and combat service support assets must be accomplished.
           A deliberate attack generally requires more assets than a hasty attack,
           as well as the time to effectively plan for them.

           5-10. Situation.

           a. To the Bradley platoon, a deliberate attack often means that the
                   enemy is alerted, ready, and dug in. It means he has coordinated
                   his artillery and has probably emplaced mines and wire. His
                  ATGMs have been carefully sighted and tanks and BFVs that
                   attempt to attack his position head on will be quickly destroyed.
                   The enemy position is often a strongpoint.

           b. To conduct a deliberate attack is a decision by the commander to
                   provide the planning and coordination time necessary to breach a
                   strongly defended enemy position even at the cost of temporarily
                   losing the momentum of the attack. A deliberate attack is
                   conducted in situations where the cost of a hasty atack will be too
                   great or because ample time has been provided to the unit with
                   which to plan and coordinate.

           5-11. Against heavy resistance.

           a. Thougha deliberate attack may be conducted against light enemy
                  resistance, it usually results from the decision to attack a well-
                  defended enemy. When a platoon or squad takes part in a de-
                  liberate attack, it does so as part of a larger force and may be
                  employed as one of the following elements:

                  (1) Breach — usually an infantry element supported by
                           engineers. Its mission is to move forward under the cover of
                           direct and indirect fire, breach the obstacles and secure the
                           far side. Though the obstacles vary, the threat normally
                            constructs his obstacle line in a set way.

(2) Assault — usually made up of tanks and mounted infantry.
      Its mission during the breaching operation is to destroy and

      suppress the enemy on the objective. Once the breachis made,
      the assault force passes through the breaching force and
      assaults the enemy positions. Infantry will normally be
      required to dismount to clear enemy bunkers and trench lines.
(3) Support — usually a tank element and BF'V element. Its
      mission is to support by firing during the breaching operation
      and the assault. This element attempts to isolate a portion of
      the enemy’s defenses by suppressing him from long overwatch

      positions. This isolation process is crucial because if a portion
      of the obstacle line is reinforced by the enemy, it will be
      difÏcult for friendly units to concentrate enough men and
      firepower to make the breach. The company team and task
       force command will also be synchronizing assets such as
      indirect fire, smoke, attack helicopters, and CAS to further

        contribute to the isolation process.

The attack starts with heavy suppressive artillery fires on known
enemy positions overwatching the breaching site. A smoke screen
is established to conceal the breaching site. The breaching force
moves forward covered by fires and concealed by smoke, and
breaches the obstacle. When the breach is made, the breaching
force marks the breach lane and secures the far side of the breach.

12. Consolidation.

  Consolidation consists of those actions taken to secure an
  objective and prepare to repel an enemy counterattack. In this
  order, the company or company team commander designates
   platoon positions and actions to be taken.

  The platoon consolidates an objective by:

   (1) Occupying the position designated in the attack order (BF Vs
          are moved into hull-down positions, if available, and
           assigned specific sectors of fire).

   (2) Establishing local security and mutual support between
           squads and adjacent platoons.

   (3) Eliminating any remaining pockets of enemy resistance and
           securing prisoners of war (PW).

   (4) Designating positions for the dismounted rifle teams if the
           commander wants them deployed away from the fighting
           vehicles. (This will normally be on a dismounted avenue of
          approach to the objective. The rifle teams prepare hasty

            fighting positions.)

13. Reorganization.

  Reorganization includes all actions taken to prepare to continue

   fighting. Reorganization should be by SOP and should include

   plans for remounting.

   (1) The squad leaders:

           (a) Replace key squad members who were lost (assistant
                    squad leader, BF'V gunner, driver).

           (b) Replace gunners of Dragons and SAWs.

                               (e) Movecasualties to a covered position, get medical aid to

                               (f) Report to the platoon leader the situation, casualties

                      (2) The platoon leader:

                               (c) Oversees evacuation of casualties.

                              (d) Requests needed resupply.

                     leadership has been lost. It may be as simple as reassigning the
                     responsibility for carrying a weapon or assigning a new sector of

                      or one or more of the BFVs have been put out of action, major
                     restructuring of the squad or platoon may be necessary to prepare
                     for future operations.

                                          Section VI. Limited Visibility Operations

             BFV infantry platoons and squads frequently will be required to
             conduct offensive operations during limited visibility. These operations
             must not be considered unusual or special. Units must train and
             operate well under all conditions.

             5-14. Purpose

             Limited visibility attacks may be conducted to retain momentum of an
             operation started in good visibility. They may be to achieve surprise,
             exploit success, or rupture strong enemy defenses. The commander
             may wish to take advantage of the fighting vehicle’s capability to
             operate during limited visibility as it will minimize the effectiveness of


---

emy antimortar fire. He may also want to gain a more favorable                     FM 7-7J —
sition to continue the attack when visibility improves.                                           5-33

-15. Equipment capabilities and limitations.

    BF'V infantry platoons and squads are better equipped for attack
    operations during limited visibility than any comparable units in
    the world.

    The driver’s night vision viewer allows him to move the BFV, and
    to sense rounds fired from turret weapons during darkness. Night
    vision goggles let the Bradley commander observe from his opened
    hatch to control movement and provide close-in security. The
    integrated sight unit’s thermal sight gives the gunner and Bradley
    commander the capability to see and engage targets under almost
    any visibility condition.

    Even though the BF'V has the capability to operate during limited
    visibility, it has limitations. The driver can see to drive, but the
    range and fixed field of his view scan limits his ability to provide
    close-in security. The gunner has excellent range with the
    integrated sight unit, but his field of view is narrow. Soldiers
    riding in the troop compartment have difÏculty observing through
    the periscopes, and they can be blinded temporarily by bright
    flashes of light caused by weapons fire and explosions. This
    results in security being limited, especially to the rear and flanks.

    Because the vehicle is relatively “blind” during darkness, the
    Bradley commander, wearing his night vision goggles, should
    observe from his opened hatch. Binoculars can also be used by
    platoon members to supplement night vision equipment.

                                                        WARNING

       Remember that to operate the turret when the hatch is open, it must be on
      combat override. The gunner and Bradley commander must remember
      that the turret weapons could pose a danger to.personnel observing from the
      cargo hatch, especially if the weapons are in the stabilized mode. The
      7.62-mm coax could be accidentally fired into the troop hatch and the
       25-mm gun could be damaged by striking it.

    Weather, smoke, and dust can lower the effectiveness of the
    platoon’s limited visibility equipment. The integrated sight unit’s
    thermal capability can be limited by heavy rain, dense fog, or
    falling snow. The TOW also is affected. In some cases, the thermal
    sight’s capability of penetrating fog or smoke exceeds the
    capability of the missile’s guidance system to track and control the


---

 —FM 7-73           missile. This means that the gunners may not be able to hit a
5-34                target with the TOW, even though the target is in range and seen
                    through the sight. The 25-mm gun and 7.62-mm coaxial machine
                    gun are not affected.

                   The effectiveness of image intensification devices (driver’s viewer,
                    Bradley commander’s goggles, starlight scopes) is reduced by
                   rain, falling snow, fog, and smoke. Since the devices also intensify
                   light from the moon and stars, the effectiveness of the devices is
                   reduced on dark nights. These visibility limitations dictate slower
                   rates of movement, require tighter formations, and limit further
                   the platoon’s flank security. The Bradley commander’s ability to
                   detect targets and control fires is reduced, and coordination
                   between the fighting vehicle element and the dismount element
                   becomes even more difÏcult.

                   Leaders should check the effectiveness of their night vision
                   equipment before an operation to determine the effects of light,
                   weather, and smoke on the equipment. Visibility conditions also
                   can change abruptly during an operation. This requires constant
                   reevaluation of equipment capabilities and limitations.

           5-16. Movement considerations.

           a. Movement is difÏcult during limited visibility. When selecting
                   movement techniques and formation, leaders must consider the
                  likelihood of enemy contact and the difÏculty of control. Distances
                  between men or vehicles usually need to be shortened to ease
                   control. Finally, leaders must guard against a false sense of
                  security by thinking darkness will conceal them. They also should
                   assume the enemy has night vision devices, and they should use
                   cover, concealment, and smoke as they would in daylight.

                  If possible, routes should be reconnoitered during good visibility.
                  If ground reconnaissance is not possible, a detailed map
                  reconnaissance is a must, keying on terrain features to be crossed
                  and distances involved. Ridgelines, railroads, creeks, and other
                  identifiable features should be used to guide on. Movement should
                  parallel rather than follow such terrain features, because the
                  enemy often will have them covered by observation and fire.
                  Friendly mortar and artillery fire can also be used to assist
                  navigation. By planning targets along the route on prominent,
                  easily recognizable terrain features, the platoon leader can call for
                  these fires as necessary. These targets are on standard features
                  that the platoon leader will avoid. This will allow him to call fora
                  specific target and verify where he is without endangering the
                 platoon.


---

  When moving dismounted, the element of surprise is the attacker’s       FM 7-75 —
  greatest advantage. Light and noise discipline must be enforced.
  When the platoon is moving mounted, the sound of the BFVs may                      5-35
  alert the enemy. The enemy may have difÏculty locating the
  platoon, because it is difÏcult to pinpoint a moving vehicle by
  sound only. Lights are a greater danger. Even blackout lights and
  filtered lights inside the vehicle are visible through the vision
  blocks and can be detected from great distances with passive night

   vision devices.

-17. Movement formations.

    Mounted.

  (1) The column and wedge formations are the easiest to control.
         The platoon leader should place his BFV as the base vehicle
         in either formation. Both formations make rapid movement
         easy by allowing the drivers to guide on the base vehicle with
         minimal supervision by the Bradley commanders.

   (2) 'the line formation is the most difÏcult to control. When the
         driver is looking through his night vision viewer to the front,
         he cannot maintain visual contact with a flank BFV.
         Therefore, the line formation should only be used to move

             short distances.

   Dismounted. Many of the considerations for mounted formations
   apply to dismounted formations. Dismounted rifle teams move
   closer together for better control. Soldiers should be close enough
   to see each other. Leaders should be near the front of the formation

    for movement control.

-18. Movement techniques.
   When visibility is limited by darkness only, the Bradley platoon
   should be able to move using any of the movement techniques,
   making only minor adjustments to formations as previously
   discussed. When smoke, fog, or falling snow limits visibility, the
   platoon’s ability to provide overwatch may be reduced. In all
   conditions of limited visibility, the loss of security to the flanks
   and rear is a major consideration in movement planning.
    A platoon moving by traveling overwatch keys its movement on
    the lead BFV. The distance between the lead BFV and the platoon


---

  — FM 7-73           is based on the ability of the driver and Bradley commander of the
5-36                  overwatch vehicles to keep the lead vehicle in sight. The
                      integrated sight unit should not be used as the primary
                      means for maintaining visual contact. Such use would
                      require the gunner and Bradley commander to watch the
                      vehicle to their front rather than to watch for the enemy.
                     When the traveling technique is used, the lack of flank security
                     becomes an even more important consideration. The wedge
                     formation allows a greater number of thermal sights to be
                     employed on the battlefield and would be the formation of choice if
                     the terrain permits.

             5-19. Attacks.

             a. Attacks during limited visibility require more detailed preparation
                    than attacks during good visibility. In limited visibility, objectives
                     are normally smaller and distances to them shorter. Plans must be
                    kept simple but complete and understood by all. If time and the
                    enemy situation permit, leaders should reconnoiter routes and
                    observe the objective area during good visibility. Indirect fire
                    should be planned for suppression and for illumination during
                    darkness. Whether the attack is mounted or dismounted, every
                    soldier should be rehearsed and questioned on his portion of the
                    plan to ensure complete understanding throughout the platoon.
                    Wire should be used as the primary means of communication until
                    contact is made.
                   There are several ways the company or company team commander
                    may attack during limited visibility. If the attack is to be done
                   during darkness, he may illuminate the battlefield using indirect
                   fire. If he wishes to take advantage of the limited visibility
                   conditions or cannot adequately illuminate the battlefield, he may
                   attack mounted, dismounting short of the objective as appropriate.
                   He may also decide to attack dismounted and use stealth to gain
                   surprise.
                   An illuminated night attack is conducted similarly to a daylight
                   attack. Even with illumination, soldiers in the troop compartment

                   cannot see well enough to fight effectively mounted. Tlumination,

                  however,makes control easier and allows rapid movement. It also
                  improves the enemy’s ability to detect advancing targets.
                  Illumination fires are planned and called as needed — normally
                  for the assault. Smoke can be used to cut down the effectiveness of
                  enemy battlefield illumination and of some of his night vision
                  devices. Indirect HE fire may be used to hide the sound of the BFVs


---

as well as to suppress enemy gunners. Thermal sights work with or      FM 7-73 —
without light equally well and should be used by the vehicle                           5-37

element as it fires into the objective.

The commander may decide to attack mounted to maintain attack
momentum against an enemy occupying hastily prepared
positions. This allows platoons to close rapidly on the objective,

and it conserves the strength of the dismount teams.

In a dismounted attack, the platoon moves mounted to the last
covered and concealed position short of the objective. The
dismount element dismounts and assaults the objective while the
fighting vehicle element provides covering fire. During the

assault, the fighting vehicle element leader must closely control

the element’s fires to avoid endangering the dismounted soldiers.
A prearranged signal, such as a pyrotechnic device, to lift and
shift fires is even more crucial in limited visibility operations
because of the inability of the gunner and Bradley commander to
clearly distinguish the friendly attacking infantry from the
enemy. As soon as the objective is seized, the vehicle element
should quickly move to the objective area. The platoon should
havea prearranged signal such as a blinking, filtered flashlight to
help the fighting vehicle element locate and join with the dismount
element. The dismount element leader should select positions on
the objective for the fighting vehicle teams, and he should require
each dismounted rifle team to provide a vehicle guide to simplify

movement into positions.

Even though a nonilluminated attack is planned, the platoon
leader should plan illumination from the LD to the objective so
that, if needed, it is available. Once the rifle teams start their
assault, illumination on the objective may help them detect targets
to fire on, and rapidly eliminate enemy resistance.

The platoon leader also should plan for the use of smoke during the
 attack. If the enemy fires illumination, the platoon leader can call

 for smoke or use the BFV exhaust smoke generators to screen

 movement. Smoke also will reduce the effectiveness of some of the

 enemy’s night vision devices.

 The main advantage gained by attacking dismounted and using
 stealth is surprise. Attacks by stealth can be conducted during any
 condition of reduced visibility. The concept of a dismounted attack
 using stealth is to get as close as possible to the enemy’s position
 without a fight — then, before he can react, to surprise and
 overwhelm him. This also allows the dismounted infantry to
 advance to a position of advantage where it can support a
 subsequent attack by tanks from a position of close overwatch

 during daylight.

  —FM 7-73     The mission of the fighting vehicle element is to support the
5-38           dismount element by fire. In the company or company team
               commander’s OPORD, the fighting vehicle element is normally
               assigned a firing position, a sector of fire, and a route to the
              objective. The firing position may be along the LD or to the rear of
              the LD. The fighting vehicle element leader designates a firing
              position and a sector of fire for each fighting vehicle team. He also
              specifies how he plans to control their fire. He then points out the
              route for the dismount element and their portion of the objective.

              The fighting vehicle element should move into the overwatch
              position during good visibility. If the noise of the vehicle will alert
              the enemy, it moves as close as it can to the overwatch position and
              halts. From there, a dismounted observer can be sent forward to
              observe the sector of fire and assist the fighting vehicles when they
              move into the position.

              Once the objective is seized, the fighting vehicle element moves as
              quickly as it can to the objective and occupies hull-down positions
             just as in a daylight attack. The dismount element should provide
             guides to lead the vehicles across the objective to their positions.

             When the company or company team commander plans a non-
             illuminated attack by stealth, he normally will use the following
             control measures.

             (1) Attack position. While the attack position is usedina
                       mounted attack, it takes on added importance in a dismounted
                      attack. It should be short of the LD, provide cover and
                       concealment, and permit easy entry and exit. The attack
                      position is occupied only long enough for the unit to receive
                      final instructions and ensure coordination.

            (2) Line of departure. An LD is designated to coordinate the
                      commitment of attacking units at a specified time of attack.

            (3) Point of departure (PD). Because it is critical that all
                      movements be closely coordinated, the dismounted rifle
                      teams are assigned a specific point to cross the LD.

            (4) Release point (RP). Each company commander releases
                      control of his platoon to the platoon leaders at the platoon RP.
                     RPs are far enough back to let units deploy before they reach
                     the probable line of deployment.

            (5) Route. The company commander normally picks the route
                    from the company RP to the platoon RP. Platoon leaders pick
                     routes from the platoon RP to the squad RP.

            (6) Probable line of deployment (PLD). The company
                     commander may designate a PLD. This is the approximate

      location where he plans to have the dismounted rifle teams                         DD

      From the PLD, the rifle teams normally begin their assault

(7) Objectives. The company commander assigns each platoon
      an objective, which is part of the company objective. These

       should be easy-to-identify terrain features.

(8) Limit of advance. To keep friendly supporting fires from
      falling on friendly dismounted troops, the company commander
      may designate a limit of advance. It should be a terrain
      feature that is easy to recognize even during limited visibility.
      The assaulting elements must not advance beyond this
      feature. This allows supporting fires beyond the objective

                       Section VII. Specialized Operations

adley platoons have the capability of operating in numerous types of
ecialized situations. BFV’s become a potent support weapon for
fantry on urban terrain. The ability of Bradley platoons to conduct
yse combat with dismounted infantry and overwatch operations with
variety of weapon systems presents the leader with numerous options

urban terrain.

addition, Bradley units will be required to utilize infiltration tactics
offset the inherent capabilities of the defender who has had time to
epare his position. The ability to infiltrate dismounted infantry toa
sition in proximity to the enemy will be critical in aiding the
netration of heavy resistance by armored forces.

20. Attacking on urban terrain.
   Offensive operations in urban areas are normally conducted by
   dismounted infantry. Tanks and BFVs follow, and are brought up
   to secure locations to provide direct-fire support. The tasks of the

   platoon in the attack of a built-up area include:

    (1) BFVs and tanks.

          (a) Isolating the objective building with direct fire to
                   prevent enemy withdrawal, reinforcement, or counter-

                      attack.
            (b) Breaching walls.
            (c) Suppressing enemy positions.
           (d) Destroying enemy positions.


---

— FM 7-73

           (e) Obscuring enemy observation, using the on-board
                    smoke generator

                    (2) Dismounted infantry.

                             (a) Assaulting and reducing enemy positions and clearing
                                      buildings under covering fires of tanks and BFVs.

                             (b) Neutralizing and destroying enemy antiarmor weapons.

                             (c) Locating targets for engagement by tanks and BFVs.

                             (d) Protecting tanks and BFVs against enemy individual
                                      antiarmor measures and surprise.

                             (e) Securing and defending an area once cleared.

           b. To accomplish tasks effectively in built-up areas, BF'V crews must
                  be able to communicate with the infantry. Arm-and-hand signals
                  will be the infantryman’s primary means of communicating with
                  the BFV. Prearranged signals or markers may indicate which
                  buildings have been cleared. Infantry must acquire targets for the
                  BFV or tank and maintain visual contact with the vehicle element
                   commander in order to relay appropriate information, such as the
                  kind of target and its location.

           c. Urban terrain offers many concealed positions from which the
                    enemy can engage tanks and BFVs at close range and from
                  different directions. Vehicles are more susceptible to fire from
                  above, below, and to the rear. Overwatching infantry fighting
                  vehicles can protect tanks and BFVs from these engagements.

           d. Standard vehicle gunnery techniques apply in urban areas;
                  however, several factors must be considered:

                   (1) Although the elevation and depression of the tank main gun,
                            25-mm gun, and coax machine gun are greater than the
                           standard threat tanks, these advantages may be offset in an
                           urban environment where battlesight gunnery will be the
                            norm, and well-placed and protected infantry antitank
                            systems in buildings will be a major threat. Vehicle
                            commanders must develop an “eye” for potential targets that
                            can and cannot be hit with vehicle weapons.

5-42


---

(2) Particular care must be taken to protect dismounted infantry        FM 7-7J —
        from the discarding parts of the armor-piercing discarding                     5-43
        sabot round and the blast overpressure of all tank main gun
        ammunitions as well as APDS residue. The tank has greater
        armor protection than the BF Vs. When contact with enemy
        armor or antitank weapons is expected, tanks should movein
        front and provide a measure of protection. The vertical
        elevation of the BFV’s 25-mm gun provides excellent direct
        fire for engaging targets in buildings above the moving
         tanks.

Adhering to the fundamental principle of mutual support, and to
reduce the dead space, the BF Vs should move in pairs on alternate
sides of the street with sectors of fire overlapping and oriented to
the other side of the street. BFVs may move by bounds within each
pair, or as a pair, depending upon the enemy situation and the
width of the street. When streets are too narrow to permit two
BFVs to pass, they should continue to operate on alternate sides;
their primary turret orientation in this situation will be directly to
the front, rather than the opposite side of the street.

Infantry should reconnoiter ahead of vehicles. This is particularly
true when a vehicle has to turn at a street corner. Drivers should be
trained to expose only the front of the vehicle and neutral steer
quickly. This enables them to fire and move forward rapidly.

Vehicle crews must be constantly aware of available defilade
positions. Corners, buildings, and rubble offer good defilade
positions; however, these may offer less protection on urban
terrain because of elevated positions available to enemy gunners.

Buildings provide both cover and concealment for vehicles. With
careful reconnaissance, excellent hull and turret-down positions
can be found. Buildings also present dangerous traps for armored
vehicles. The following steps must be followed:

(1) Infantry clears the structure from rooftop to basement and
         provides continuous all-round security to prevent enemy
         infiltration for a close-in kill.

(2) Never enter a building with a basement if there is any doubt
        that the ground floor can hold the vehicle’s weight.

(3) Enter througha rear wall to permit hasty withdrawal under
        pressure. Remember to protect the gun system. This may
        mean traversing the 25-mm gun over the rear deck before
        hitting the wall and creating the entry hole. The vehicle then
        backs out, traversing the turret, and entering the building to
         assume a firing position.


---

—FM 7-73

                  Tanks and BFVs can reduce exposure to enemy fire by moving
                  rapidly across streets. The three to five seconds involved may
                  often be too short for the enemy to acquire, shoot, and hit a moving
                  vehicle.

          5-21. Infiltration.

          a. The ability of the BFV’s dismounted infantry to infiltrate into a
                  position of advantage before an attack by tanks and BFVs offers
                  several important tactical options, especially in the deliberate
                 attack.

              . When time is available, an infantry force can be infiltrated
                 through the enemy obstacle line to a position of advantage near
                 the enemy’s flank or rear. From such a position, a dismounted
                 platoon or company can support a subsequent attack by tanks or
                 BFVs either by fire or assault. In both cases, the objective of the
                 dismounted element is to use terrain (covered and concealed route)
                 or limited visibility (haze, smoke, night) to position itself to attack
                 and unhinge the enemy defense at a time and place that supports
                 the attack by the tanks or BF Vs. In addition, infiltration offers one
                 of the means by which friendly units can overcome enemy forces
                 defending built-up areas.

                 The considerations for an infiltration operation include:

                 (1) Time to position dismount infantry before the attack by tanks
                          and BFVs.

                 (2) Ability to use terrain and limited visibility to conceal the
                          infiltration.

                 (3) Coordination between the infiltration force and armored
                         vehicle force before the departure of the dismounted infantry.

                 (4) Ability to navigate to a specific preselected position, probably
                          under reduced visibility.

5-44

                                                              CHAPTER 6

                                              Defense

he purpose of defensive operations is to repel an enemy attack and destroy the
tacker. Defensive operations may also be undertaken to hold critical terrain,
gain time, or to wear down the enemy. The platoon defends as part of a
mpany or company team and completes tasks assigned to it by the company
‘company team commander.

                               Section !. Planning the Defense

he defense may involve fast, frequent movement between battle
sitions and during counterattacks. Platoons and squads must be
ple to respond to short-notice changes in mission and must be able to
sht immediately from a new battle position. Thus, platoons must
evelop and practice SOPs, master applicable drills, and learn to
<ploit the mobility and firepower of the fighting vehicle.

                                                                                                                                                                               6-1
