——FM 7-73

           6-1. Defensive tasks.

           The platoons defend to hold terrain and destroy the enemy. Their
           defensive tasks include:
           a. Destroying enemy BMPs, BTRs, and other lightly armored

                   vehicles with the 25-mm gun and with Dragons, LAWs, and
                   grenade launchers.
                   Destroying enemy tanks with the BFV-mounted TOW and with
                   Dragons and LAWs.
                  Suppressing enemy antitank fires with the 25-mm gun, grenade
                  launchers, 7.62-mm coaxial machine gun, SAWs, and rifles.
                   Repelling dismounted enemy attacks with the BFV and dismounted
                   infantry.
                   Locating the enemy and providing security by manning observation
                   posts and conducting patrols and ambushes.
                   Building obstacles to slow, stop, or canalize the enemy and
                   providing security for obstacles.
                   Conducting platoon-size counterattacks, or as part of larger force,
                   to regain a portion of their position that has been overrun.

           6-2. Operation order.

           a. When the platoon’s mission is to defend, the company or company
                  team commander must explain his plan for the defense. He does
                  this by issuing an operation order. From the order, the platoon
                  leader learns:
                  (1) The most likely and most dangerous enemy avenue of ap-
                           proach and expected enemy course of action.
                  (2) The platoon’s mission.
                  (3) The company team and battalion task force commander’s
                           concept, or commander’s intent, of how the defense will be
                           fought.
                  (4) The position of the platoon in the company or company team
                           defense.
                  (5) The platoon’s sector of fire or engagement area.
                  (6) The fire support that is available.
                  (7) The on-order missions for the platoon.


---

                                                                                                                                                      FM 7-73 —

   (8) The evacuation or destruction procedures for damaged

            vehicles.

   (9) The evacuation procedures for friendly casualties.

 (10) The place where prisoners of war are to be taken.
 (11) The availability of ammunition, mines, barrier materials,

            and other supplies.

  (12) The special signals that are to be used.

   On receipt of acompany operation order,the platoon leader begins
   his troop leading procedures (discussed in Chapter 3). He begins
   with an analysis of the mission, enemy, terrain, troops, and time

    available.

   Often, the platoon leader will have to issue simple, fragmentary
   orders and rely heavily on SOPs because the tactical situation

   requires immediate action. During occupation of a battle position,
   the platoon and squads should use the applicable drills to reduce
   time and possible confusion. Regardless of the time available, the
   platoon leader should do as many of the troop leading procedures

    as possible.

   When the platoon leader has completed his analysis, made his
   reconnaissance, and developed his plan, he then completes his
   order. The order should follow the standard five-paragraph
   operation order format and be issued orally. Where possible, SOPs
   should be referred to in the order. This helps to shorten the order.
   When possible, the platoon leader should give his order from a
   point overlooking (or on) the platoon’s defensive position. The
   order must explain what is to be done, how, when, and by whom.
    The squad leaders then give orders to their squads.

-3. Priority of tasks.
    To help the platoon use available time efÏciently, the leader
    should establish task priorities. Normally, these are in the SOP,
    but they can be modified as necessary by the platoon leader or
    company commander. In most situations, the tasks are:

     (1) Establish security.
             (a) Establish OPs.

          (b) Conduct local patrols to search for enemy stay-behind

                    forces, sensors, mines, or booby traps.

                                                                                                                                                                                6-3


---

—FM 7-7J

                 (c) Position M8 alarm.
                 (d) Maintain one-third of troops on security at all times.

          (2) Position key weapons (location, sectors of fire, PDF, FPF).
                   (a) BFVs.

                 (b) Dragons.

                 (c) M60 or SAWs.

          (3) Clear fields of fire and prepare range cards and sector
                  sketches.

          (4) Prepare primary fighting positions.

          (5) Emplace hasty minefield/obstacle system.

          (6) Establish local communications system (wire, trenches).
                   (a) BFVs.

                 (b) Fighting positions.

                 (c) OPs.

          (7) Emplace PEWS, night vision equipment, and other warning
                  devices (higher priority during limited visibility).

          (8) Improve fighting positions.

                 (a) Overhead cover.

                 (b) Aiming stakes.

                 (c) Camouflage.

                 (d) Bury land lines.

                 (e) Hide or dispose of fresh earth.

            (9)  Prepare alternate and supplementary positions.
          (10)
                 Stockpile ammunition, water and food, and conduct
                 maintenance.

          Some of these tasks should be done at the same time. The platoon
          leader and squad leaders must closely supervise the activities to
          ensure that valuable time is not lost on tasks of minor priority.
          The first 30 minutes of the occupation of a defensive position are
          critical because during this period security is established,
          positions are designated, and work is begun. The platoon leader
          must conduct a hasty reconnaissance to ensure that the location of
          his position is correct and that the squad sectors and key weapons
          positions will not have to be relocated once they are in place.


---

                                                                           FM 7-73 —

  The platoon leader should coordinate with both flank units and
  with his company team commander early enough to preclude
  having to move his squads or make major adjustment in fighting
  positions after construction is well under way. Squad leaders

   coordinate on their flanks as well.

  Constant supervision of the preparation of defensive positions is
  necessary, especially the verification of squad sectors and key
  weapons positions and fields of fire. If it becomes obvious to a
  platoon or squad that a sector must be adjusted or that positions
  must be shifted, the decision should be made quickly and the

   soldiers moved where they are needed most.

  Rest, sleep, and eating plans should be made so that security and
  work can continue, but not all personnel are exhausted when the

   enemy attacks.

-4. Indirect fire planning.

   Most indirect fire planning is done by the company commander
   and the fire support team chief with input from the platoons. A
   copy of the target list is given to the platoon leader. The platoon
   leader and his FO check the target list to ensure that fire is planned
   on all enemy avenues of approach and on known or likely enemy
   positions in the platoon sector of fire. If more targets are needed,
   the FO requests them through the FSO. The FO normally stays
   with the dismounted element since he has virtually no capability
   to call and adjust indirect fires when mounted.
   At platoon level, fires should be planned to the front, on top, and to
   the rear of platoon positions. In each of these areas (front, top,
   rear), fires are planned on likely enemy avenues of approach and
   on prominent terrain features from which fires may be adjusted.
   In addition, fires are planned on dead space that cannot be

    adequately covered by other platoon weapons.

   Fire planning is a team effort between the platoon leader and his
   FO. It usually occurs after the rifle team sector sketches and BFV
   range cards have been compiled and the platoon leader has
   determined where his defensive plan requires strengthening. At
   platoon level, he selects a few critical targets that he and his other
    key leaders can easily identify during the battle.
   When the platoon leader, with the aid of his FO, determines which
    targets are to be covered by indirect fire, the coordinates
   (eight-digit, if possible) are determined and the information is


---

—FM 7-7J

                 passed to the company team FSO who compiles all of the platoon
                 fire plans for the company commander. Eventually, the confirmed
                 target list is returned to the platoon where the FO quickly confirms
                 the targets by plotting them on the map since the company
                 commander may have added or deleted some targets. Once the
                 confirmed targets have been plotted on the map, they are matched
                 to the terrain and then disseminated among key personnel (PSG,
                 RATELO).

          e. The guide for how many targets a platoon leader should request is
                 based on his ability to call for them during the battle. Generally, he
                 should attempt to memorize the target numbers for all of the
                 indirect targets in his platoon sector. This will allow him to quickly
                 call for those fires during the battle without having to refer to a
                 map or reference card and without having to rely on light if the
                 fight takes place during limited visibility. Normally, a few targets
                 are sufÏcient in a platoon sector, especially if they are on
                 prominent terrain features from which they can be adjusted.

          f. The company commander may assign a mortar or artillery final
                 protective fire (FPF) to a platoon. An FPF is a prearranged barrier
                 of fire. A platoon leader must plan the FPF location with his FO
                 and the FSO. It should cover the most threatening dismounted
                 approach. The FPF is planned close to the platoon position, but not
                 close enough to endanger friendly troops. The FO will advise the
                 platoon leader on how close to the rifle teams an FPF can be fired
                 with no danger to the troops. This varies with the type of weapon
                 and ammunition fired. When assigned an FPF, the platoon leader
                 will have authority to call for it unless the company commander
                 retains authority. The FPF is essentially fired as a last resort
                 to stop an enemy assault. On order, it is fired continuously until
                 itis ordered stopped. All other platoon weapons fire while the FPF
                 is being fired.

3-5. Obstacle planning.                                                       FM 7-73 —
                                                                                                6-7
Le The platoon has little organic capability to emplace significant
     obstacles but can enhance its sector and individual positions in a
     number of ways.

     (1) Mines can be carried on the BFVs and a hasty protective
              minefield can be emplaced.

     (2) Tactical wire can be carried on the BFVs and used either for
               protection or as a deception to confuse the enemy as to exact
              position locations.

     (3) Trip flares, Claymores, and field expedient tangle foot
              obstacles can be emplaced.

     (4) Trees can becut using pioneer tools, and field expedient
              abatis and roadblocks can be constructed.

      If a platoon leader receives or is told he will receive engineer
      support in his area, he should still put in those obstacles that he is
     capable of emplacing with his own assets and then prioritize those
      projects that require outside assistance. In many cases, engineer
      assets will be executing specific engineer missions in the platoon
     area that have been directed by higher headquarters. In these
     cases, the platoon leader should verify that the obstacles fit into
     his platoon defensive plan and if not should coordinate with the
     engineer element or the company team commander.

      Once engineer obstacles have been emplaced, the platoon leader
     should review his platoon obstacle plan to determine if any
     adjustments of his own hasty protective obstacles are required.

     Obstacles, once emplaced, must be covered by observation and
     fire. If not observed and covered by fire, they will be easily
     breached or bypassed, especially during limited visibility.

-6. Defensive sector sketch.

     The leaders of the fighting vehicle crews prepare BFV range cards
     (DA Form 5517-R) and squad leaders prepare sector sketches.
     (Each antiarmor specialist and automatic rifleman prepares a
     range card.) Thesketches and range cards serve as memory aids to
     the platoon and help the platoon leader prepare his platoon
     fire plan.

     A rifle team sector sketch is a rough drawing, as close to scale as
     possible, showing:

     (1) Main terrain features in the sector and the range to each.

     (2) Each primary position.


---

— FM 7-73

           (3) Engagement areas or primary and secondary sectors of fire
                    for each position.

           (4) SAW or M60 FPLs or PDFs.
           (5) Type of weapon in each position.
           (6) OP and leader positions.
           (7) TRPs in the sector.
           (8) Dead space.
           (9) Obstacles.

           c. The sketch should be prepared based on direct observation of the
                  sector and by using each weapon’s range card. (See Appendix C for
                  explanation of range card preparation.) Two copies of the sketch
                  should be made. One copy goes to the platoon leader. The other
                   copy remains at the position.

. Coordination between adjacent
      platoons/squads/teams.

Platoon leaders coordinate with adjacent platoons. Squad leaders
coordinate with adjacent teams so that all positions and all units
are mutually supporting. The platoon leader checks to ensure that
this coordination has taken place. Coordination normally is
initiated from left to right. Gaps between positions are covered by
fire as a minimum and coordinating points are established to
ensure that units meet at some specific point on the ground to tie in
their flanks.

Information exchanged includes:
(1) Locations of primary, alternate, and supplementary positions;

         and sectors of fire for BF Vs, SAWs, and Dragons.
(2) Location of dead space between units and how it is to be

         covered.

           6-8. Planning for remount.

           a. Because Bradley platoons will dismount their infantry in the
                  defense, the remount must be planned in detail. This is especially
                   true where subsequent movement is an integral part of th
                  defensive plan and especially when the dismount and vehicl.
                  elements are separated for the fight. The inability to plan anc
                   execute a speedy remount causes the advantage of the BFV’s speec
                  to be negated as the vehicles are forced to wait for the dismountec
                  infantry to linkup and remount.

          b. Planning for the remount at platoon level should include:
                   (1) Remount location.
                  (2) Reconnaissance of route to the remount point by both the
                           vehicle and dismount elements.
                  (3) Marking of the route to the remount point.
                  (4) Signals to initiate the remount and contingencies for:
                           (a) Limited visibility.
                           (b) Loss of communications.
                           (c) Loss of leaders.

                                Section Il. Defensive Tactics and Techniques

          The platoon’s defense must capitalize on the BFV’s firepower, armor
          protection, agility, thermal vision equipment, and the dismounted
          infantryman’s fighting capability.


---

   BFVs are best positioned to defend against enemy mounted                FM 7-7J —
   attacks along mounted avenues of approach.                                         6-13

   Rifle teams are best positioned to defend against enemy dismounted
   attacks along avenues that restrict mounted movement or on the
   reverse slopes of mounted avenues of approach where they can
   deliver surprise fires at the effective ranges of their LAWs and
   Dragons against enemy vehicles and not be subjected to long-
   range suppression by the enemy.

9. Basic tactics.

   The BFV offers defensive employment options not previously
   available to the combined arms team. The capable and sophisticated
   turret weapons of the BFV allow it to fight against the enemy in its
   own right, while the dismounted infantry can be used in restrictive
   terrain to their best advantage.

   Bradley units are capable of fixing or substantially limiting the
   movement of the attacking enemy, thus allowing tanks to be
   consolidated and deliver a powerful counterattack.

   The fixing of the enemy — denying him the ability to withdraw
   part of his force for employment elsewhere — by Bradley units is
   done by the BFVs using their enhanced firepower and maneuver-
   ability while the dismounted infantry digs in on restrictive terrain
   or on a reverse slope and fully exploits the advantage of the
   defender to prepare the battlefield. As with the offense, when
   dismount occurs, a fundamental change in the command and
   control structure takes place. Although the platoon leader remains
   in overall control of both the vehicles and dismounted infantry, he
   retains direct control of the maneuver element and turns over
  functional control of the other element to the platoon sergeant.
  One leader concentrates on fighting the dismount element to take
   advantage of restrictive terrain and orients his fight to dismounted
   tactics while the other takes control of the vehicles and concentrates
  on the BFV fight. Though at times these two elements (dismounted
  element and mounted element) may separate from each other, they
   must fight in relation to one another.

  The BFV’s anti-BMP, antitank, and antipersonnel firing systems
  combined with its survivability must be optimized through the use
  of:

  (1) Movement.

  (2) Cover and concealment.

  (3) Dispersion.


---

—FM 7-73         (4) Mutual support.
6-14
                 (5) Flank shots.

                 (6) Stand-off range.

                 (7) Employment in depth.

          6-10. Methods of employment.

          a. There are three basic methods of employment for the Bradley
                 platoon: same battle position, same avenue of approach; same
                 battle position, different avenues of approach; different battle
                 positions, same avenue of approach.

                 (1) BFVs and dismounted infantry on the same battle position
                          covering the same avenue of approach.

                           (a) Using this method, the platoon can defend against
                                    mounted and dismounted attacks and move rapidly to
                                    another position.

                          (b) Within the battle position, the BFV may be positioned
                                    with the rifle teams forward or around the vehicles for
                                   security. Normally, if the dismounted avenue of ap-
                                   proach is the most dangerous to the platoon and the
                                    terrain is restrictive, the BF Vs will be positioned based
                                    on their ability to employ the 7.62-mm coax in support
                                    of the dismounted positions. Otherwise, the BF Vs are
                                   positioned to take advantage of their long-range fires
                                    and the infantry either provides them security or takes
                                    up positions on a reverse slope.

                          (c) TheBFVs remain on thesame battle position as the rifle
                                   teams when the terrain provides good observation,
                                   fields of fire, and cover and concealment to both
                                   dismounted infantry and BFVs. In addition, the battle
                                   position must provide fields of fire that take advantage
                                   of the restrictive terrain that dismounted infantry
                                   prefers and/or provide protection for the dismounted
                                    infantry from the long range fires of the enemy.

                          (d) The platoon leader assigns each vehicle and rifle team a
                                   primary position and sector of fire. He should also
                                    assign alternate positions particularly with the BFVs.
                                   The platoon leader designates who will man OPs and
                                   gives a general location for each OP. OPs are eventually
                                   adjusted to better fit into the company team reconnais-
                                   sance and surveillance (R&S) plan.


---

—                                                                    FM 7-7J —

    (e) The platoon leader supervises the positioning of each
            vehicle, ensuring that it ties in with other vehicles
            according to his concept of the defense. Often this
            means that the vehicles are offset to the flanks to get
            better long-range shots.

    (f) Employing both elements of the Bradley platoon on the
            same battle position covering the same avenue of
            approach is often a conservative use of the Bradley
            platoon. Its primary advantages are:

    ® Facilitates command and control functions within
          the platoon because of the proximity of both the
          vehicle and dismount elements as well as their ori-
          entation on the same approaching enemy.

    ® Facilitates remounting of vehicles.

    © Provides increased security for the BFVs because of
          the proximity of friendly dismounted troops.

   (3) BFVs and dismounted infantry on different battle positions
          covering the same avenue of approach.

           (a) If positioned on separate battle positions, BFVs and
                   dismounted infantry must fight in relation to each other
                   and cover the same avenues of approach. Fighting in
                   relation to one another means that the BFVs are able to
                    provide the dismounted infantry with supporting fires
                    from their primary, alternate, or supplementary positions.
                    Both elements are positioned to engage enemy forces on
                    the same avenue of approach, but at different ranges.
                   This will normally equate to a maximum of three-fourths
                   of the effective range (approximately 2,000 meters) of
                   the BFV’s primary armament — the 25-mm gun. This
                   ensures that the BF'V fires can reach and overlap the
                   dismount positions. As long as they are fighting in
                   relation to each other, the platoon leader will normally
                    continue to control both elements.

               ¢ The dismount element should use available time to
                     prepare fighting positions and obstacles. When the
                     enemy attacks, the BFVs normally will engage
                     enemy formations and, at a prearranged signal or
                     event, move to alternate positions to the flank or to
                    the rear of the dismount element. The timing of this
                     move is critical. Whilemaximum advantagecan

---

element forward, the vehicles become more and more       FM 7-7J —
vulnerable to enemy fire as the enemy closes.                       6-19

Since the fighting vehicle element will be the first to
see and engage the enemy, and timing of movement
to alternate or subsequent positions is critical, the
platoon leader normally commands the fighting
vehicle element and the platoon sergeant is the
dismount element leader. Sometimes, tactical
considerations dictate other methods. For example,
when the primary fight is expected to be dismounted,
the platoon leader would stay forward with the dis-
mounted element. As the situation develops, the
platoon leader may move to the fighting vehicle ele-
ment or to a position where he can better control
both elements. This allows the platoon leader to stay
abreast of the situation and still provide maximum
control where the primary fight is expected. Control
is most difÏcult when the elements are separated.
The commander may tell the platoon leader which
element to locate with.

The leader of the dismounted element must be able to
plan operations that are conducted without the
support of his vehicles. The quantity and type of
weapons, ammunition, mines, equipment, and
supplies to be with the dismount element must be
considered. How long the teams will operate sepa-
rately and how quickly the rifle teams must be
able to remount are also important planning
considerations.

The BFVs may be employed well forward to perform
a specific mission. When the mission is completed,
the BFVs displace to a position to support the
dismount element. This method may be used when
the commander wants to use the BFVs for long-range
antiarmor engagements well forward of the dismount
element’s positions. In such fights, the BFVs must
avoid decisive engagements so they can displace to
their next positions. Rifle teams are positioned in the
rear toimprove positions and emplace obstacles.
Once the BFVs have displaced to the rear, they can
fight using any of the methods discussed earlier.

                     (1) A company or company team commander may consolidate
                              the company’s dismount elements in one location and deploy
                              the platoon’s BFVs separately in the following situations:

                              (a) A large number of dismounted troops are required to
                                        hold a position, for example, a strongpoint.

                              (b) Primary position for the dismount element does not
                                       allow adequate fields of fire for the BFV’s weapons.

                               (c) The dismount element must occupy heavily wooded or
                                        rugged terrain that the BFV cannot traverse.

                             (d) When both a mounted and dismounted avenue of
                                         approach must be defended and the terrain is such that
                                      both cannot be defended from the same battle position.

                     (2) In this case, the dismounted infantry and BFVs may not be
                             able to support each other initially but plans should be made
                             to incorporate the BF V’s speed to reposition them to support
                             the dismounted infantry from supplementary or subsequent
                             positions.

                    (3) During limited visibility, the company or company team
                             commander may modify his plans to provide additional
                             security for the fighting vehicle element. This can be done by
                              movinga rifle team to the fighting vehicle element’s position
                             or by rejoining the platoon on a single battle position.

            6-11. Reverse slope defense.

            a. The estimate of the situation will often require the company team
                    commander to employ his elements, especially his dismounted
                   infantry, on the reverse slope. If the factors of METT-T require the
                   employment of dismounted infantry on what is essentially a
                   mounted avenue of approach, the dismounted infantry must be
                   concealed from the enemy at ranges beyond which their own
                    weapons are effective. This means that dismounted infantry
                   should be protected from enemy tank gun and observed artillery
                   fire. This applies even when friendly forces are fighting with their


---

tanks and long-range ATGMs. Ideally, dismounted infantry              FM 7-7J —
should be deployed so that they are not vulnerable to fire from                      6-21
enemy direct fire systems they cannot effectively engage with

their own weapons.

The majority of dismounted infantry weapons are not effective
beyond 600 meters. In order to reduce or preclude destruction from
enemy direct and indirect fires beyond that range, a reverse slope
defense should be considered.

This conflicts, to some extent, with the need for the maximum
observation forward to adjust indirect fire on the enemy as well as
the need for long-range fields of fire for friendly tanks, BFVs, and
ATGMs. In some cases, it may be necessary for tanks, BFVs, and
ATGMs to be deployed forward while the dismounted infantry
remain on the reverse slope. These vehicles withdraw from their
forward positions as the battle closes and enemy artillery becomes
effective. The vehicles’ new positions should be selected to take
advantage of the BF Vs’ long-range fires to get enfilade shots from
the depth and the flanks of the reverse slope.

At night, the nature of the threat may change and dismounted
infantry may occupy the forward slope or crest to deny it to the
enemy. In those circumstances, it is feasible for a dismounted
element to have an alternate night position forward.

The area forward of the crest must be controlled by friendly forces
through aggressive patrolling and active as well as passive
reconnaissance means. The enemy must not be allowed to take
advantage of reduced observation to advance to a position of
advantage without being taken under fire.

There are several advantages to a reverse slope defense.

 (1) Enemy ground observation of the position including the use
         of surveillance devices and radar is masked.

 (2) Enemy cannot engage the position with direct fire without
         coming within range of the defender’s weapons.

 (3) Enemy indirect fire will be less effective owing to the dif-
         ficulty of observation.

 (4) Enemy may be deceived about strength and location of the

          positions.


---

 —FM 7-73   (5) Defenders will have more freedom of movement out of sight of
6-22                the enemy.

           There are several disadvantages to a reverse slope defense.
            (1) Observation to the front is limited.
            (2) Fields of fire to the front are reduced.

            (3) Enemy is able to launch his attack from a closer range.

           The decision to position forces on a reverse slope is normally made
           by the company team commander. He will normally position
           forces on a reverse slope when:

           (1) A unit wishes to surprise or deceive the enemy about the
                    location of its defensive position.

           (2) A forward slope might be made untenable by direct enemy
                    fire.

           (3) Occupation of the forward slope is not essential to achieve
                   depth and mutual support.

           (4) The fields of fire on the reverse slope are better or at least
                   sufÏcient to accomplish the mission.

           (5) The forward slope position is likely to be the target of
                   concentrated enemy artillery fires.

           The BFV offers the unit additional opportunities regarding
           positioning that were not possible before. BFVs can initially be
           positioned forward to take advantage of their protection from
           artillery and their ability to engage the enemy at long ranges.
           After an initial engagement, BFVs may move over or around the
           crest line and through the dismounted infantry on the reverse
           slope to a position that is either on the flanks or farther in depth to
           the rear.

           Obstacles are also necessary in a reverse slope defense. Since the
           enemy will be engaged at close range by the units on the reverse
           slope, obstacles should be emplaced that:
           (1) Prevent the enemy from closing too quickly and overrunning

                   the positions.

           (2) Facilitate disengagement if decisive engagement is not
                   desired.

6-24
              a. The firepower and long-range accuracy of the 25-mm gun and
                     TOW on the BFV are among the platoon’s greatest assets. Based

                     of METT-T, the platoon leader selects positions for his BFVs.
                     Ideally, each vehicle’s position provides:
                     (1) Cover, especially to the front.
                     (2) Concealment from enemy ground and air observation.

             b. Each vehicle should have a primary position and as many
                    alternate positions as needed to cover the entire sector of fire.
                    Supplementary positions should be designated by the company
                     team commander or platoon leader to cover secondary sectors of
                    fire or the next most dangerous avenue of approach. If the BFVs
                    are fighting separated from the dismounted infantry, they must be
                   able to support those positions. All three weapon systems (25-mm
                    gun, TOW, 7.62-mm coaxial machine gun) should be considered
                   when positions are selected and prepared; however, the platoon

                   and within 175 meters. The plastic sabot falls away from the

                   unprotected personnel. The same is true for tank’s main gun sabot
                   ammunition out to a distance of 1,000 meters and 70 meters on

                   (1) TOWs can kill tanks out to 3,750 meters. This is beyond the
                            maximum effective range of threat main tank guns (usually
                           between 1,500 and 2,000 meters). This gives the BFV a
                            stand-off advantage with the TOW. This advantage should
                           be exploited when possible. TOW positions must offer
                           unobstructed fields of fire and a clear backblast area and
                            must fire from a level place of terrain.

                  (2) The TOW missile has a high kill probability on any tank it
                          hits. This kill probability rises if the TOW hits the tank’s

---

                                                                         FM 7-73 —

Av          because a tank crew’s observation and the tank’s main gun
            are normally oriented to the front. Thus, a side or flank
            engagement reduces the chances of being detected while it
            improves the chances of a kill.

    The BFV cannot survive against antiarmor missiles or fire from
    direct fire weapons larger than 14.5-mm. The two ways the vehicle
    can overcome this vulnerability is to stay concealed and deliver
    surprise fire on enemy tanks or other armored vehicles from the
    flanks and rear or engage at the maximum ranges of the TOW
    (3,750 meters) or 25-mm (2,200 meters) and displacing to alternate
    positions before the enemy can place effective fire on the BFV.
    This movement to alternate positions should be covered by fire by
    the other BFVs in the fighting vehicle element. In this way, the
    enemy is placed under a constant stream of fire and is not allowed
    to acquire and engage targets.

    The enemy will attempt to suppress the vehicles with direct and
    indirect fire and smoke. The fighting vehicle element should be
    positioned to get as much separation as possible between BFVs
    while still mutually supporting each other. This reduces the
    chances of two or more BF'Vs being suppressed by the same enemy
    fires. (A good planning figure is approximately 100 meters
    between vehicles.)

    Hide positions, especially out of the direct fire line of the enemy
    should be the norm for BFVs in the defense, not only do they
    provide protection to the BFVs, but they also conceal the true
    location of the positions thus allowing for surprise fires on the
    enemy. Firing positions (hull down, if possible) should be prepared
    when time permits and movement from hide positions to firing
    positions should be rehearsed. If the BFVs are collocated with the
    rifle teams, the dismounted infantrymen can observe the sector
    and call the vehicles forward to preselected firing positions when
    enemy targets are in firing range. The hide-position technique
    may be used by individual BFVs or by the entire platoon. If the
    elements are separated, the fighting vehicle eiement leader may
    have to dismount and move forward to observe the sector.

    The use of hide positions helps avoid early detection by enemy
    ground and air forces. Routes from hide positions to firing
    positions should be concealed so that the vehicles moving forward
    will not be detected and engaged by the enemy. Communications
    between the observers and fighting vehicle element can be by
    prearranged visual signals, wire, or radio. By having several
    firing positions for a single hide position, each BF'V is able to
    engage targets at long ranges with the TOW and 25-mm gun and

Hull-down positions should be occupied whenever possible. In
such positions, only the turret is exposed to enemy fire, and the
hull is protected by cover. By camouflaging the turret, the BF'V is
then difÏcult to detect, but turret weapons can be fired. When first
occupying a hull-down position, the 25-mm gun should be fully
depressed to ensure that close-in targets can be engaged without
moving the vehicle.

                                                         BFV HULL DOWN

Additional protection is provided to the BFV by placing it in a
turret-down position. In this position, the vehicle is in a position
that gives cover to the front, but the vehicle commander can still
see what is to his front. The best way to move into this type of
position is to have the driver move up to a hull-down position,
where the vehicle will fight, and then have the gunner direct him
in reverse until the gunner can no longer see through his sights. At
that point, the turret will be covered from the front. To engage, all
that has to occur is for the driver to move the vehicle forward until
the gunner indicates he has fields of fire.

           a. Rifle teams are best employed against the most dangerous enemy

                           therefore, the platoon leader must plan for the possibility that
                           his rifle teams may have to fight both a mounted and
                           dismounted enemy threat. Restrictive mounted approaches,

                           natural obstacles, are areas well suited for the rifle team’s
                           defense against a mounted enemy.

                            approach is wide, then it may become necessary to occupy

hen the enemy attacks, BFVs designated to engage at long range,

-14. How fighting vehicle elements defend.

    The BFV-equipped platoon can defend better against a greater
    variety of threats than previous mechanized platoons. With the
    BFV and its 25-mm gun, TOW, and 7.62-mm coaxial machine
    gun, infantry can now defeat mounted attacks at longer ranges
    and win the close-in fight.

     (1) TOW.

            (a) Primary targets for the TOW are enemy tanks. Because
                   of the small number of TOW rounds on the BFV, it is


---

  — FM 7-73                      critical not to waste missiles on targets that can be
6-36                             killed by other weapons. The basic rule for TOW use
                                 is to engage enemy tanks as soon as they are in range
                                 and on the flanks. Accurate preparation of a range card
                                 aids the gunners and Bradley commanders in deter-
                                 mining that enough exposure time is available for a hit.

                       (b) When a TOWis fired, the BFV must move to an alter-
                                 nate firing position to avoid enemy return fire. Once two
                                TOWs have been fired, the launcher must be reloaded.
                                The BFV should move to a hide position, reload, and
                                then move to an alternate firing position. The platoon
                                leader must be kept informed of missiles on hand for
                               firing. The platoon leader or platoon sergeant should
                                request resupply during any lull in the battle, even if
                                only a few missiles are needed.

             (2) 25-mm gun. The 25-mm gun, firing APDS ammunition, can

                      defeat the BMP1 and other light armored vehicles (BTR,
                      BRDM) out to 2,200 meters. By engaging BTRs and BMPs as
                      they come into range within the platoon position, the
                      defender can separate the enemy infantry from his tanks by
                      forcing him to dismount. Once dismounted, the enemy
                      infantry is vulnerable to small arms and indirect fires. The
                       25-mm gun can continue to engage BTRs or BMPs, or switch
                      to HEI-T to destroy or suppress dismounted infantry or thin-
                      skinned vehicles. As with the TOW, time to reload the
                       weapons system must be planned. APDS should be reserved
                      for targets that cannot be killed with HEI-T. Also, HEI-T
                      should be held for targets that cannot be killed or suppressed
                      with the 7.62-mm coaxial machine gun. HEI-T and APDS
                      should be reloaded at every chance to avoid running out of
                      ammunition during an enemy attack. Adding ammunition to
                      existing links is quicker than loading empty weapons. When
                      changing from one type of 25-mm ammunition to another, the
                      first round fired will be of the type previously selected because
                      that round is already chambered.

             (3) 7.62-mm coaxial machine gun.

                      (a) The coaxial machine gun is effective in suppressing
                               ATGMs and enemy machine gun positions, defeating
                               thin-skinned vehicles, forcing armored vehicles to
                               button up, and engaging troops on foot or riding on the
                               outside of tanks. The 7.62-mm coaxial machine gun


---

                        should be used whenever possible to conserve the larger   FM 7-7J —
                        caliber ammunition.                                                   6-37

               (b) Keeping the coaxial machine gun at maximum ammu-
                        nition load is just as critical as for the 25-mm gun. It
                        should be reloaded to capacity at every chance.

b. The BFV leader moves to an alternate firing position to avoid
      effective enemy fire or to gain a better firing position in the desired
       sector of fire or engagement area.

      (1) This movement may be directed by the fighting vehicle
               element leader or may be done automatically by the squad
               leader if his position has been discovered and targeted by the
               enemy. The fighting vehicle crew must avoid multiple
               engagements from the same firing position when the
               enemy is returning effective fire. Movement of individual
               vehicles must be coordinated so that all vehicles will not be
               out of firing positions at the same time. Normally, movement
               to supplementary positions is directed by the platoon leader.
              This movement normally involves all parts of the fighting
               vehicle element moving at the same time, but it may be done
               by single BFVs or by pairs.

       (2) If effective enemy fire forces a BF'V to leave its position, the
              onboard smoke-grenade launchers or smoke-screen genera-
               tor can be used to conceal the vehicle’s movement.

c. Ifthe platoon is ordered to move to another battle position, and if
      its elements are located together, the fighting vehicle element may
      continue the fight while the rifle teams remount the vehicles.
      When the elements are separated, the dismount element should
      notify the fighting vehicle element leader before movement to the
      remount point. The BF'V then moves to the remount point to pick
      them up. If either element becomes decisively engaged, then the
      platoon must disengage. To avoid decisive engagement, the pla-
      toon must move quickly. An enemy force traveling at 20 kilome-
      ters per hour moves | kilometer in only three minutes. To slow the
      enemy, the fighting vehicle element increases its rate of fire and
      the FO adjusts for indirect fire and smoke on the enemy. Emplaced
      barriers and mines also will slow the enemy attack. The BFV’s
      smoke-screen generators, if needed, can be used to supplement the
      smoke provided by indirect fire. Remounting considerations are
      explained in greater detail in Section V, Disengagement.

  —FM 7-7J  6-15. How dismounted elements defend.
6-38
              a. Defending against a dismounted attack. During an attack,
                    the enemy infantry will advance as far as possible mounted in
                    BTRs and BMPs. When forced to dismount, usually 300-400 meters
                    from our position, the infantry will continue the attack on foot
                    supported by indirect fire, tanks, BTRs, and BMPs. Indirect fires
                    should be placed as fast as possible on the enemy’s dismounted
                    forces.

                    (1) The dismounted elements should engage the attacking ene-
                             my force as soon as it comes within the element’s sector of
                             fire. Targets in the primary sector of fire have priority. But,
                             when no targets show in the primary sector, targets in the
                            secondary sectors are engaged.

                    (2) As the enemy begins the assault, the platoon leader and his
                            FO should call for all FPF's. A heavy stream of fire is main-
                             tained until the enemy assault is halted. The rate of fire is
                            then reduced to save ammunition.

                    (3) When the enemy assault is repelled, the platoon leader re-
                            organizes his positions. He gets a status report from each
                            squad, ensures that key weapons are manned, designates
                            replacements for key leaders, and reports his status to the
                             company team commander. Retreating enemy forces are
                            often disorganized and exposed to fire. The platoon leader
                            should keep calling for indirect fire and be prepared to quickly
                            remount the BFVs and counterattack, if ordered to do so.

            b. Dismounted infantry defending against a mounted attack.
                   Riflemen and SAW gunners should direct their fires at exposed
                   crew members to force them to close their hatches, and at dis-
                   mounted infantry moving along with the tanks. If the enemy
                   infantry can be separated from his tanks, the tanks become vul-
                   nerable to infantry antiarmor weapons.

                   (1) Dragons are used to engage enemy tanks as soon as the tanks
                            enter their sectors of fire. They may be fired at enemy tanks in
                            secondary sectors of fire when no tanks are seen in primary
                            sectors of fire. When engaging targets, antiarmor specialists
                            should make maximum use of the frontal protection of their —
                            positions and try for flank shots at target tanks. Dragon |
                            engagements should be controlled by squad leaders because
                            of the scarcity of ammunition.

-16. Preparing for the next attack.

Nhen an enemy assault is repelled, leaders must prepare to counterattack,
o continue the defense in place, or to displace. If the platoon leader is
lirected to hold his present positions, the platoon must quickly prepare

or more enemy attacks. The platoon must:

                                                                                                                                             6-39


---

 —FM 7-73   a. Reestablish security. If OPs withdrew to the battle position,
6-40               they are sent back out. If any of the OP personnel did not return
                    or are wounded, they must be accounted for or replaced.

            b. Replace key personnel. If there are casualties among leaders or
                   critical weapon operators, they are replaced.

            c. Redistribute/resupply ammunition. Squad leaders inventory
                   and redistribute remaining ammunition. Ammunition from casu-
                   alties is redistributed. If the squad vehicle is nearby, the rifle team
                   gets additional ammunition from the vehicle. Ammunition status
                   is reported to the dismount element or platoon leader. Fighting
                   vehicle crew leaders reload the 25-mm gun and 7.62-mm coaxial
                   machine gun and make a quick count of remaining ammunition
                   and missiles. Ammunition and missile status is reported to the
                   vehicle element or platoon leader.The fighting vehicle element
                   leader may also redistribute ammunition and missiles among the
                   BFVs. The platoon leader or platoon sergeant consolidates the
                   platoon’s ammunition status reports, and then requests resupply.
                   If necessary, he will send a vehicle to pick up more ammunition
                   and missiles.

           d. Evacuate the dead and seriously wounded, and enemy PWs.
                   The wounded are treated and, when possible, returned to duty. The
                   seriously wounded are evacuated to the rear. After casualties are
                   evacuated, all sectors of fire must be checked to ensure they are
                   still covered. Leaders must ensure that positions are readjusted, as
                  needed, to cover any gaps left by casualties or disabled BFVs.
                  Enemy prisoners are evacuated to the rear, after a quick inter-
                   rogation and search for information that might be of immediate
                  value to the platoon.

           e. Replace camouflage. When the situation allows, wilted material
                  is removed and replaced with fresh camouflage. A position should
                  not be overcamouflaged.

           f. Replace obstacles. If enemy forces have withdrawn, obstacles, |
                  mines, and early warning devices should be replaced. This is a
                  risky task, especially if there are enemy snipers around. Troops—.
                  must be careful; smoke can be used to cover movement. Obstacles _

               may have to be ‘replaced after dark.

           6-17. Counterattack.

           During the conduct of defensive operations, leaders at all levels must.
           seek opportunities to attack. The counterattack is an excellent way to|

           seize the initiative, to destroy or disrupt the enemy, or to gain key.

           terrain.


---

    Platoons normally counterattack to regain all or a portion of the         FM 7-7J —
    platoon position. These counterattacks are often done by massing                         6-41
    direct fires and calling for indirect fires to eject the enemy from
    the position before he can establish himself. Counterattack by
    maneuver is often done with only a few men, especially if other
    portions of the platoon position are still defending. If the BFVs
    are nearby, they can be used to fire or maneuver to aid in restor-
     ing the platoon position.

    The platoon sometimes counterattacks as part of a company,
    company team, or battalion task force. Some counterattacks are
    planned in great detail. Others, like hasty attacks, are not planned
    but are executed rapidly when the right conditions exist. Counter-
    attacking forces must complete their tasks and regain covered
    positions before overwatching or following enemy echelons can
     interfere.

    At the platoon level, counterattacks may resemble a hasty attack.
    Platoon leaders make an estimate of the situation and react
    immediately to catch the enemy at a weak point. The preferred
    method of counterattacking involves repositioning a unit so that
    effective fire can be placed on the enemy (counterattack by fire). In
    this case, the unit moves only to the extent necessary to attack by
    fire. However, at times it may be necessary to assault the enemy
    and drive him off a piece of terrain. This situation is normally
    associated with the enemy seizing a part or all of the platoon’s
    defensive positions. To restore the continuity of the defense, the
    enemy must be expelled. This requires decisive action to hit the
     enemy before he has an opportunity to react.

    The platoon leader’s decision to counterattack must not be reck-
    less. It must involve an understanding of the higher (company)
    commandeyr’s intent and the use of good judgment before taking a
    calculated risk. For example, the company commander may des-
    cribe the necessity of retaining a specific piece of terrain that is
    critical to the battalion’s defensive plan. If this terrain is lost, but
    can be regained through the immediate action of a platoon, the
    platoon leader should seize the initiative and retake the terrain.
    Where feasible, the platoon leader should take action based on the
    commander’s direction; however,in the absence of specific orders,
    the platoon leader should have the latitude to take the initiative.

                       Section IV. Limited Visibility Operations

fechanized infantry platoons and squads frequently will be required
» conduct defensive operations during limited visibility; therefore,
hese operations should be emphasized during training exercises. This


---

  —FM 7-73  section provides doctrinal guidance on the conduct of defensive
6-42        operations when visibility is limited.

            6-18. Limited visibility considerations.

            a. Limited visibility conditions refer to darkness, fog, rain, smoke,
                    dust, or any battlefield obscurants that may be employed. These
                    conditions may require the use of image intensifiers, thermal
                    sights, binoculars, and artificial illumination. Some devices, such
                    as image intensifiers and thermal sights, should be used together
                    so that the capabilities of one system can offset the disadvantages
                    of the other. During heavy rain, snow, fog, smoke, and dust, the
                   effectiveness of night vision devices will be degraded, and
                    increased security measures must be implemented, such as the
                   establishment of more observation posts, patrols, and remote
                    sensors (see Appendix N).

                   Limited visibility conditions afford platoons and squads some
                    concealment from enemy observation and reconnaissance. To
                   maximize the advantages of limited visibility, individual soldiers
                   and leaders must consider several factors.

                   (1) Atnight, objects may appear distorted. Ranges are difÏcult to
                            estimate and dark objects appear more distant than light
                            objects. To compensate for these conditions, use either the
                             scanning or off-center viewing techniques outlined in FM
                            21-75, Chapter 4. On a clear night, the naked eye can
                            distinguish land relief and coloration up to 400 meters. With
                             a full moon, the naked eye can spot a moving man at
                             approximately 240 meters and with the aid of binoculars, at
                            700 meters. Haze, smoke, dust, and fog limit observation
                            further.

                   (2) During daylight, haze, smoke, and fog may prevent the use of
                           image intensification devices. Also, the effectiveness of
                           thermal sights is degraded. Provisions for day limited
                            visibility operations must be made. Range cards must be
                            prepared so that personnel can cover main avenues of ap-
                            proach and obstacles.

                   (3) Physical and psychological factors must also be considered
                            in limited visibility operations. Darkness may stimulate the
                            imagination and thus burden the nervous system, creating a
                            feeling of insecurity that could lead to panic. The sensitivity
                            of the eyes and ears during night differs from day. Soldiers
                            using STANO devices should have the opportunity to rest at
                           least every 30 minutes. To avoid eye fatigue, operators should
                           be rotated every 1 1/2 to 2 hours. Platoon and squad sleep


---

             plans should be established and enforced; otherwise, the in-  FM 7-7J —
              dividual soldier’s fighting ability will be degraded.                    6-43

    (4) At night, sound can be heard farther, but the direction of
             sound is difÏcult to determine.

-19. Positions.

    When occupying a battle position during good visibility, the
    platoon leader must be prepared for limited visibility by
    predesignating positions for vehicles and crew-served weapons.
    Whenever possible, vehicles and crew-served weapons should be
    placed in positions that will preclude repositioning for limited
    visibility conditions. If repositioning of vehicles and crew-served
    weapons is necessary, the distance these weapon systems are to be
    moved must be kept to a minimum. The routes to be taken and
    positions to be used during limited visibility must be predesignated,
    and the movement must be rehearsed during good visibility.
    Dragons’ thermal sights have limited capability to fire through
    smoke and haze.

    During limited visibility, a platoon leader may have to reposition
    rifle teams and BF'Vs closer to designated engagement areas. The
    use of alternate engagement areas may be necessary to acquire
    targets if the assigned engagement area will be beyond the range
    of observation. Another reason for repositioning forces is to cover
    gaps between units or to cover alternate avenues of approach that
    are created by the reduced effectiveness of weapon systems.

    The repositioning of forces, if necessary, should take place soon
    after the beginning of limited visibility conditions. Moves are
    along previously reconnoitered routes into predesignated posi-
    tions.

-20. Command and control.

    The basic command and control consideration at platoon level is
    control and synchronization of the vehicle and dismount
    elements. Since the platoon leader normally locates with the
    maneuver element, if one is used it will most likely be the mounted
    element. The platoon sergeant will then locate with the dismount
    element.

    In the defense, command and control are vital and the most
    difÏcult to achieve and maintain under limited visibility
    conditions. Good command and control begins in the fighting


---

—FM 7-73

                                               controlling fires.

                                               (1) Aiming stakes — used to assist the soldier in firing his
                                                        weapon on dangerous avenues of approach.

                                               (2) Sector stakes — used on the right and left to define the
                                                        sector of fire. They also prevent accidental firing into
                                                       adjacent positions.

                c. The use of range cards and squad and platoon sector sketches for
                        control is essential. It is through the integration of such control
                        measures that a coordinated defense is possible. Target reference
                        points (TRPs) are especially necessary for the 25-mm and TOW
                        systems because of the difÏculty of estimating distances at long

                       be used to mark or verify TRPs.

-21. Coordination.

   Proper coordination must be made with adjacent platoons that are
   on the left and right flank of the platoon’s battle position. This
   coordination includes the sectors of fire for night firing of
   crew-served and vehicular weapon systems, repositioning of
    forces during limited visibility, and security measures necessary
    to secure the front and flanks.
   The platoon leader must position his STANO equipment and night
   vision devices so that overlapping fields of observation are
    established within the platoon’s sector of fire.
   The capabilities of the integrated sight unit must be realized. It is
    important that this system be manned and that a surveillance
    plan be implemented to ensure that sectors of observation overlap.
    Operation of the ISU requires starting the engine of the Bradley
    approximately every two hours to keep the batteries charged. All
    Bradleys should be started at the same time to prevent the enemy
    from knowing how many vehicles are on the position (see
    Appendix N for silent watch technique).

-22. Occupying a defensive position.

    Generally, the techniques used to occupy a defensive position
    during good visibility apply during limited visibility. Because of
    problems of command and control, whenever possible, the dis-
    mount element and BFVs should be placed on the same battle

     position.

   A defensive position to be occupied should first be reconnoitered
    during good visibility. Both the reconnaissance and the occupation
    must be done with stealth and under enforced light and noise

     discipline.

    During the reconnaissance, the platoon leader:
    (1) Ensures that no enemy forces occupy the proposed battle

              position.

    (2) Identifies enemy avenues of approach (mounted and dis-
            mounted) and potential enemy overwatch positions.


---

 —FM 7-73    (3) Chooses engagement areas if they are not assigned by the
6-46                   company commander.

             (4) Chooses primary, alternate, and supplementary positions for
                      the rifle teams and fighting vehicles.

             (5) Identifies dead space in front of positions and formulates a
                      plan on how to cover it.

            (6) Chooses locations for observation posts and the command
                       post.

            (7) Confirms locations of adjacent platoons and companies.
            (8) Chooses target reference points, sectors of fire, and other con-

                     trol measures.

            (9) Chooses routes into and out of positions.

            A reconnaissance conducted during limited visibility must
            accomplish the same objectives as above. Because of the limited
            range of observation, the platoon leader’s task must be accomplished
            with great care. He must ensure that his reconnaissance is done
            with aSTANO device of similar capabilities as that of his weapon
            systems.

            If time permits, the platoon leader should go forward, conduct his
            reconnaissance, return to the platoon position, and bring the
            squad leaders forward in his BFV. Heshould assign rifle team and
            fighting vehicle positions, sectors of fire, TRPs, and engagement
            areas. The squad leaders should then return to the platoon position
            and issue orders for the occupation and preparation of forward
            positions. The platoon then moves forward.

           If there is not enough time for the tasks above, the platoon leader
           may take his squad leaders forward during the initial reconnais-
           sance, or bring the entire platoon forward to an assembly area in
           the vicinity of the defensive position, and then conduct his
           reconnaissance with his squad leaders.

           As the platoon members occupy the defensive positions, they ac-
           complish the work priorities.

           The platoon leader must carefully consider the method of
           employing the dismount element and the BFVs. Whether to fight


---

       both elements from different battle positions or the same battle      FM 7-73 —
       position must be closely examined. During limited visibility, the                   6-47
       occupation of battle positions and the controlling of fires is
       simplified if both elements are on the same battle position.

i. Allactivities normally associated with the occupation of defensive
       positions during good visibility are done during limited visibility.
       However, techniques may change to compensate for the limited
       visibility condition, such as having to use night vision devices to
       establish sectors of fire, and actually walking the FPL and PDF.
       Noise and light discipline must be strictly enforced. Also,
       face-to-face coordination with adjacent platoons must be conducted
       and sectors of fire coordinated. This coordination should
       effectively tie in overlapping sectors of fire and observation with
       weapon systems and night vision devices. When good visibility
      returns, defensive positions are adjusted as necessary.

                                        Section V. Disengagement

As the enemy closes, and based on orders from the task force
commander, the company or company team commander will decide
how long to hold defensive positions. The company or company team
may be required to remain and fight as long as possible, or it may be
required to disengage and displace to subsequent positions. A platoon,
as part of a company or company team, may break contact with the
enemy to defend from another battle position, to prepare fora
counterattack, to delay, to withdraw, or to prepare for some other
mission.

6-23. Fire and movement.

a. Fire and movement to the rear is the basic tactic for disengaging.
      All available fires are used to stop the enemy and allow platoons to
       move away from the enemy. The company or company team
       commander may move his platoon and mass fire to stop or slow the
       enemy advance before beginning the movement away from the
       enemy. A heavy volume of antiarmor fire will force the enemy to
       dismount his infantry and thus slow his mounted advance. Ar-
      tillery and mortar HE fire and smoke will also add to the enemy’s
       confusion, slow the momentum of his mounted attack, and help
       conceal the movement of friendly units. Small arms and indirect
      fire can be used against an attack by dismounted troops.

                   while other units move to break contact.

    (3) Fire and movement is repeated until contact with the enemy             FM 7-7J —
          is broken, until the units pass through a higher level                               6-49
           base-of-fire force, or until the units are in the next position to

             resume their defense.

    When facing a mounted enemy attack, antiarmor weapons are the
    most effective weapons for the base of fire. For that reason,
    movement of those antiarmor weapons must be closely controlled.
    Normally, ITVs move back first, followed by BFVs, then tanks.

     In restrictive terrain, when facing a dismounted enemy attack, or
     with visibility limited, the ITVs and tanks may have to move first,
     covered by the infantry and their BFVs.

     The tactics used by the platoon to disengage from the enemy can
     differ according to how the platoon is deployed, the company or
    company team plan for disengagement, and other factors; but
     some actions apply in all cases:

     (1) Maximum use is made of the fighting vehicle’s firepower to

              cover rearward movement.

    (2) BFVsshould back out of position and move, keeping a terrain

             feature between the vehicle and the enemy.

     (3) The turret weapons should remain pointed in the direction of
           the enemy. Firing port weapons should be manned and ready
           to fire, especially from the rear firing ports. This is critical
            when the squad is operating at reduced strength.

     (4) Rapid movement and an effective base of fire are the keys toa

               successful disengagement.

6-24. Plans for a disengagement.
a. Plans for a disengagement may be part of any defensive plan. If

     rifle teams are deployed, a plan for rapid remounting must be
     made. Keeping the platoon mounted or placing the rifle teams with

      the fighting vehicles simplifies this process.

3-25. How the dismount element disengages.
When the dismount and fighting vehicle elements are separated, there
are three ways the dismount element can disengage. Simultaneous
lisengagement (moving all teams at the same time) can be used when
‘he element is covered by another force. When the dismount element
must cover its own movement, it disengages by teams or by thinning

the lines.
a4. Simultaneous disengagement.

     (1) When the rifle teams simultaneously disengage, they
           assemble and move as one element as fast as possible to the
             remount point, using movement techniques.

     (2) Simultaneous disengagement is favored when rapid move-
            ment is critical, the disengaging element is adequately
            covered by overwatching fires, and the enemy has not closed
            on the dismount element or cannot fire effectively at it or
            there are significant obstacles to delay the enemy. Simultaneous
             disengagement can be used when the dismount element can
            move before the enemy can close on the position because of an
            obstacle or distance between the dismount element and the
            enemy. It can also be used when other units of the company,
           company team, or battalion task force are adequately

                covering the disengagement.

b. Disengagement by rifle teams.
      (1) When the dismount element must cover its own movement,

            one or two teams stay in position as a base of fire. The rest of
            the dismount element moves to the rear. Teams left in


---

— FM 7-73

                                            position must fire into the entire element’s sector to cover the
                                            movement of the other rifle teams. Sectors of fire are adjusted
                                             as necessary to get better coverage of the element’s sector.

                                  (2) The teams left in position disengage when the rest of the
                                           element is in position to cover their disengagement.

                                  (3) Movement to the rear by alternating teams is continued until
                                            contact is broken. Once contact with the enemy is broken, the
                                           disengagement is complete and the dismount element moves
                                           to the remount point using proper movement techniques.

                                  (4) Disengagement by rifle teams has the advantage of simplicity
                                          in that the rifle teams stay together. It is used when one or two
                                           teams can effectively cover the entire dismount element’s
                                            sector.

6-54                   BFVs. When the BFVs and the rifle teams are employed on the
                       same position, the rifle teams normally move to the rear while the
                       BF'Vs provide a base of fire. The BFVs then quickly move to the
                       rear, link up with the infantry, load them and move out. The rifle
                       teams can use any of the disengaging techniques discussed earlier.
                      The method selected usually will be dictated by the enemy
                      situation, the terrain, the fighting vehicle crews’ ability to serve as
                       a base of fire, and the type and amount of overwatching fires.

              6-26. Howthe fighting vehicle element disengages.

              Because of the BFV’s speed, firepower, and protection against small
              arms fire and artillery shell fragments, it is usually best for the
              dismount element (when deployed) to disengage first while covered by
              the BFVs. But, ifthe BFVs are not in a position to support the dismount
              element by fire or, if the dismount element is heavily engaged, the
              fighting vehicle element may have to disengage first and move to a
             position to assist the dismount element in disengagement. Whichever
             method is used, there are two basic ways the vehicle element can
             disengage. If the BFVs are covered by another force, simultaneous
             disengagement may be used. If the BFV must cover its own movement,
             it disengages by pairs. These methods are similar in concept to those
             used by the dismount element.

             a. Simultaneous disengagement. When the BFVs disengage
                     simultaneously, they move as one unit as quickly as possible. This
                     method is normally used when the BFVs are covered by another
                     force and speed is the most critical factor. If the rifle teams are
                     already mounted, the entire platoon moves, using movement
                     techniques, to a position designated by the company or team
                     commander. If the rifle teams are deployed, the BFVs move to the
                     remount point to pick up the rifle teams, or it may have to attack |
                     the enemy by fire from a new position to allow the rifle teams to
                     disengage. Once the rifle teams have disengaged, the BFVs again
                     disengage either simultaneously or by the method described
                    below, as the situation warrants.

             b. Disengagement by vehicle or pairs of vehicles.

                     (1) When the BFVs must cover their own disengagement, one,
                              two, or three vehicles can be left in position as a base of fire
                             while the remainder moves to the rear. The BFVs left in
                             position must cover the entire sector until the moving
                             vehicles reach positions they can use to provide a base of fire.

            (3) The BFVs receiving the heaviest tank and ATGM fire are
