                                          SOUND

                 Sound communications include such
           simple devices as whistles, horns, gongs, and
           explosives. Sound signals are used mainly to
           attract attention, transmit prearranged mes-
           sages, and spread alarms. Sound signals
           work but only for short distances. Battle
           noises cut down the range and reliability of
           sound-signals. They are also open to enemy
           interception, so their use may be restricted for
           security. To avoid any misunderstanding,
           sound signals must be simple. They are
           usually prescribed by unit SOP and the
           CEOI.

                                     MESSENGER

                 Using a messenger is a fairly secure
           means of communicating and usually the
           best way to send long messages that cannot
           be delivered personally by a commander. It
           is, though, the slowest means of sending
           information and is vulnerable should the
           messenger be delayed, captured, or killed.

                  Messages sent by a messenger should be
           clear, concise, and complete. No unnecessary
           words should be used. If there is a chance the
           messenger might be captured, the message
           should be in code using the operational code
           in the CEOI.

                                             WIRE

                  Wire communications should be used
           whenever the platoon expects to stay in one

         the fighting vehicle element and the dis-

         fighting vehicle crews and rifle teams by

                Because the rifle teams use TA-1s, one
         strand of the wire must be cut, the insulation
         stripped back, and the wires attached to the
         binding posts of the TA-1 to connect the rifle
         teams to the wire net. Because one strand of

         which means that if the wire is broken or

                                                                                RADIO

                                                      Because Threat forces have an extensive
                                               radio intercept capability, radio is used
                                               within the platoon only when messages
                                               cannot adequately be sent by other means. If
                                               a radio transmission is intercepted, the
                                               enemy can usually find out where a unit is
                                               and what it is doing.

                                                      When radios are used, transmissions
                                               must be short and to the point. The sender
                                               must know what he wants to say before he
                                               transmits. This helps to keep messages short
                                               and the radio net open for others to use. Also,
                                               it reduces vulnerability to enemy intercept.

                                                      Each vehicle in the platoon mounts an
                                               AN/GRC-160. The platoon leader’s and pla-
                                               toon sergeant’s vehicles also mount an
                                               AN/VRC-46.

                                               AN/VRC-46. The AN/VRC-46 radio is
                                               powered by the vehicle’s electrical system. Its
                                               principal advantage is its 41-kilometer
                                               planning range. If it or any other vehicular

Secure Ramp and Ramp Door. The ramp               FM 7-7J—
and ramp door should be firmly closed and                          E-3

                          FORDING

      The entry site should be firm; have a
gradual slope (maximum of 30 percent or 17
degrees); and be free of rocks, stumps, deep

drops, and underwater obstacles. The vehicle

driver should ease the BF'V into the water to
prevent water from rushing back from a bow
wave and swamping the hatches. When the
vehicle is level, the driver should slowly drive
the vehicle as he would on dry land.

       If the vehicle begins to float and loses
traction, the driver should continue to drive
using the swimming procedures (explained
in section II) until the vehicle regains its

 traction.

       As the vehicle nears the exit point, the
 driver again should slow down. If there is an
 abrupt rise or ledge, the driver may not be
 able to see, so the track commander should
 give him instructions to get the vehicle out of

 the water.

                    AFTER FORDING

      To avoid congestion, the vehicle should
 be moved away from the exit point to its
 assigned area or to continue its mission. The

 BFV needs no special after-fording care.

  —FM 7-7J

 SECTION II. SWIMMING WITH THE BFV

                                                                                                                          GENERAL

                                                                                                    When platoons and squads are required
                                                                                                to cross bodies of water deeper than 3.5 feet
                                                                                                (1.05 meters), they must prepare the vehicle
                                                                                                for swimming. There are three major steps in
                                                                                             the swimming process — preparing the
                                                                                               vehicle, swimming the water obstacle, and
                                                                                                  restoring the vehicle to its normal fighting
                                                                                            form.

                                                                                                          PREPARING THE VEHICLE

                                                                                                    When platoons and squads prepare their
                                                                                            vehicles for swimming, they should doitina
                                                                                               covered and concealed location within a
                                                                                               short driving distance to the swim site. The
                                                                                                  route to the swim site should be free of dense
                                                                                               underbrush to prevent damage to the water
                                                                                            barrier. There are several actions to take
                                                                                            before swimming.

                                                                                            Position the Turret. The turret weapons
                                                                                            should be oriented at 6400 mils azimuth
                                                                                                  (straight ahead) with the 25-mm gun and the
                                                                                                  7.62-mm coaxial machine gun elevated to +30
                                                                                            degrees. (The TOW launcher is not erected or
                                                                                            elevated.) After the water barrier is erected,
                                                                                            the weapons can be lowered.

                                                                                              Prepare Firing Ports. The firing port
                                                                                                     weapons should be removed and plugs
                                                                                              emplaced into each weapon’s ball socket.
                                                                                           Firing port vent levers should be closed.
                                                                                           These seal all the firing port openings and
                                                                                                        prevent water from entering the vehicle
                                                                                           through these holes.

                                                                                                 Prepare Drain Plugs. The two drain plugs
                                                                                              underneath the hull and the two in the final
                                                                                           drives must be tightened to get a proper seal
                                                                                                 so water will not enter the vehicle. The four
                                                                                              upper drain plugs MUST BE REMOVED.
                                                                                           These plugs allow water that gets inside the
                                                                                              water barrier to drain into the bilge so that it
                                                                                           can be pumped free of the vehicle by the bilge

                                                                                                                                               pumps.

                                                  FM 7-7J—

limitations are based on the design of the
BFV and its swim barriers but they do not
consider the effects of unstable or poor
traction on river banks. Water-entry speed
must be limited to 5 miles per hour to prevent
damage to the trim vane structure. The driver
should ease up on the accelerator. This is one
of the most crucial points in swimming. If
only one track makes ground contact, the
vehicle can be thrown off course and become
swamped if the tracks are moving too fast.
The driver should try to touch bottom with
both tracks at the same time. When both
tracks have enough traction for normal
steering, the driver can drive the vehicle out
of the water. The Bradley commander will
have to give the driver detailed instructions,
because the driver cannot see over the trim
vane and water barrier.

 drain plug access covers should be lifted and

E-10        holes on the road wheels, idler wheels, and

            should be checked for contaminated oil. The
            oil is contaminated if bubbles appear in it or

                     SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
                        FOR SWIMMING THE BFV

                    Before swimming the BF'V in any peace-
            time operation, and when possible in combat
            situations, the vehicle should be predipped.
           This check insures that the vehicle is safe
            and ready to swim. The vehicle is readied for
            swimming as explained earlier. A cable from
            a medium recovery vehicle M88 should be
            attached to the BFV’s tow pintle. The vehicle
           then enters the water until afloat. Soldiers in
           the troop compartment should check for
           leaks. The Bradley commander should check
           to see that the bilge pumps work. If all is well,
           the vehicle backs out of the water. If it has
           movement problems, the M88 will tow it.

                   Each BFV should be checked before
           swimming operations to insure that its
           intercom system and radio work.

                   Personnel in the vehicle should not wear
           seat belts while the vehicle is swimming. The
           belts could hinder safe exit if the vehicle
           begins to sink or does sink.

                  Every man should wear an inflatable life
           jacket. Life vests are not issued with BFVs.
           They must be provided by support elements.
           THE LIFE JACKET SHOULD NEVER BE
           INFLATED INSIDE THE VEHICLE. It
           should be inflated only when the soldier is
           free of the vehicle.

                  Personnel in the vehicle should not wear
           load-carrying equipment, packs, or pistol
           belts while the vehicle is swimming. Such
           items may snag in the vehicle as a soldier
           tries to get out of a sinking vehicle.

                      HOVERING HELICOPTER

                 If a hovering helicopter is picked up by
         the Bradley commander or gunner, the
         aircraft is engaged with the 25-mm gun using
         the gunner’s integrated sight unit. Range to
         the target is estimated by using the stadia
         lines in the sight reticle, making a quick
         check of the map for the target’s location and
         range, using reference points whose range is
         already known, or estimating the range and
         adjusting the rounds until they hit the target.
         The Hind is approximately the same height

as a BMP when measured from the bottom of

Using the integrated sight unit is more

coaxial machine gun. Bursts of 25 rounds of
HEI-T (APDS for Hinds) are fired at 200
rounds per minute. The gunner aims slightly
above the fuselage. At longer ranges, tracers
may appear to be striking the target when

      During the move, the platoon must be         FM 7-73 —
prepared to take action if attacked by enemy                        G-5
air, artillery, or ground forces. Passive
measures against enemy air include main-
taining proper interval between vehicles,
staggering vehicle positions within the
column to avoid linear patterns, camou-
flaging vehicles, and maintaining air ob-

servation.

      If attacked by enemy air, vehicles in the
column move from the axis of attack, either
occupying covered and concealed positions
or continuing to move, maintaining an
evasive course. The unit also engages the
aircraft with all available weapons.

      If the column receives indirect fire during
the move, button up the vehicle, mask, and
move rapidly out of the impact area. Masking
is necessary because the enemy can use a mix
of HE and chemical ammunition to disrupt
movement and achieve maximum casualties.
After the company team is through the
impact area, the march unit commander will
start unmasking procedures.

      If engaged by enemy ground forces while
on a tactical road march, vehicles attempt to
continue movement, or the platoon leader
may elect to assault the enemy or fix the
enemy for other forces to attack.

      Because the primary mission of the unit
is to move to a new location in preparation for
future operations, additional actions against
ground forces depend on the size of the enemy
 force and instructions from the company
 team/march unit commanders. If the enemy
 force consists of snipers or other disruptive
 forces equipped with small arms, the com-
 mander may pass through the force or
 dispatch a platoon to eliminate it. If the force
 is larger and presents a danger to the task
 force as a whole, fragmentary orders may be
 issued for march units to leave the route of
 march, move to covered and concealed
 positions, and conduct a hasty attack as if
 conducting a movement to contact.

                            magazine-fed, gas-operated weapon. It has a
                            selector lever that allows the rifle to be fired
                            semiautomatic or automatic. The most stable
                            firing positions (those increasing the prob-
                            ability of target hits) are the prone supported
                            or foxhole supported for semiautomatic fire.

    — FM 7-7J     first LAW, he notes its impact. Ifhe gets a hit,
H-8               he continues to shoot using the same sight

                                              Pair Firing

                         One at a time, two or more gunners with
                 two or more LAWs shoot at a target. Each

                 gunner prepares several LAWs. The gunners

                 swap information when shooting at the
                 target. The first gunner seeing a target
                identifies it, announces the estimated range
                and lead he will use (for example, TANK, 150
                 METERS, FAST TARGET) and shoots. If
                the first gunner has a miss, the second
                 gunner quickly announces a revised estimate
                of range and lead (if appropriate) and shoots.
                The gunners continue exchanging range and
                lead information until one gets a hit. Once
                the range and lead have been found, all
                gunners, on command, shoot at the target
                until it is destroyed. Pair firing is preferred
                over sequence firing as it lets gunners get
                target hits faster; that is, gunners firing the
                subsequent shots can be ready to shoot as
                soon as the previous round impacts. In
                sequence firing, the gunner must get another
                LAW, establish a sight picture, and shoot.
                Pair firing also has the advantage of having
                two or more gunners track the same target.

                                          Volley Firing

                       Two or more gunners with one or more
               LAWs shoot at a target at the same time.
               Shots are fired on command or on signal until
               the target is destroyed (for example, TANK,
               100 METERS, SLOW TARGET, VOLLEY
               FIRE, READY, AIM, FIRE). Each gunner

               prepares two or more LAWs. Volley firing is

               used only when the range to the target and
               the lead have been determined. Range can be
               determined by map, by pacing, or from the
               results of pair firing after a target has been
               hit. The volley firing method is best because

   — FM 7-7J                   M47 DRAGON MEDIUM
H-10                             ANTITANK WEAPON

                General. The Dragon is a line-of-sight wire-
                guided missile system. In its lightest con-
                figuration, it has two major components, the
                tracker and the ammunition. The ammuni-
                tion consists of the launcher with the missile
                package inside. The launcher is the handling
                and carrying container as well as the tube for
                firing the missile. The tracker is the reusable
                part of the system. The launcher is destroyed
               and discarded after firing.

               Firing the Dragon. To fire the Dragon, the
               antiarmor specialist looks through the sight
               and puts the crosshairs on the target. He
               keeps the crosshairs on the target and fires.
               By keeping the crosshairs on the target, the
               missile is guided to the target by the wire link.

               The tracker detects deviations from the

               gunner to target, line of sight, and direction
               of the missile, and sends corrections to the
               missile system,. The missile system responds
               to corrections by firing jets along its sides to
               change its direction.

               Firing Configurations. The Dragon is
               fired dismounted using the bipod or tripod
               mounts.

                                    Dismounted Bipod

                      When establishing a hasty defense or
              when used in dismounted movement, the
              Dragon may be fired using the bipod
              attached to the launch tube. Using this
              method, the Dragon gunner takes a sitting
              position with the weapon on his shoulder.
              The tracker crosshairs are kept on target by
              moving the shoulder and body.

                                   Dismounted Tripod

                      When equipped with the M175 mount,
              the cradle and damper assembly can be
              installed on an M3 (caliber .50 machine gun)
              tripod, or an M122 (M60 machine gun) tripod,
              by using the tripod adapter. The tripod

                                                 control problems, and leaders must recognize
                                                 and overcome every problem that makes it

                                                 tween friendly and enemy units, fire weapons
                                                 effectively, and navigate.

            Move Vehicle to Safe Location. If the
            vehicle can move under its own power, it
            should be moved to a safe place before
            evacuating casualties. If the driver is
            wounded and cannot operate the vehicle, he
            should be removed through the troop
            compartment, replaced, and the vehicle
            driven to a safe location.

            Check and Treat Casualty. Too rapid an
            evacuation of a casualty may cause further
            injury. Before a casualty is evacuated, he
            should be checked thoroughly to discover the
            full extent of his injuries, and first aid should
            be administered to those wounds requiring
            attention. There may be some instances,
            though, when the casualty should be evacu-
            ated immediately (such as a burning vehicle).

           Evacuate Casualty. After giving the
           necessary first aid, the casualty’s CVC
           helmet or headset should be disconnected
           and his seat belt released. If the vehicle is on
           its side or overturned, he must be supported
           before the seat belt is released, to prevent
           additional injuries. He is then evacuated.

                         SAFETY PRECAUTIONS

                   The Bradley commander, gunner, and
           driver should stow their load carrying
           equipment (LCE) under their seats. This
           action lets them move about the vehicle and
           get out of it without the LCE catching on
           objects in the vehicle. This also helps others
           to evacuate them if they become casualties.

                   Before evacuation, the LCE should be
           removed from casualties in the troop com-
           partment so that the equipment does not
           catch on anything during evacuation.

— FM 7-7J

                          BRADLEY COMMANDER
                                     AND GUNNER

                    The way the Bradley commander and
            gunner will be evacuated will vary depending
            on whether one or both are casualties, and
            whether or not the turret is operable.

                    If the turret is operable and only one
            person is injured, the uninjured person will
            rotate the turret to 6400 mils to align the
            turret opening with the turret shield door.
            The turret drive power should then be turned
            off to prevent the turret from moving during
            evacuation. The uninjured person will un-
            buckle and disconnect both CVC helmets.
            The injured person is rotated to the center of
            the turret and pulled from his seat. He is
           guided through the shield opening, moved
            into the troop compartment, and taken out by
            the ramp.

                   If the turret cannot be rotated to align the
           turret shield door with the turret opening, the
           evacuation must be through the turret
           hatches.

                   The uninjured person opens both turret
           hatches and raises the seat of the injured
           person to the full up position. He then
           unbuckles the injured person’s seat belt and
           disconnects his CVC helmet. Two persons
           outside the turret lean in and pull the injured
           man out through the hatch. A pistol belt may
           be used as outlined earlier. The man inside
           the turret assists in lifting and guiding the
           injured person through the hatch. Once
           outside the turret, the two men lower the
           injured man down to others on the ground.

                  If the vehicle is on its side, the injured
           person’s CVC helmet is disconnected and his
           seat belt released. He must be supported
           before the seat belt is released, to prevent
           further injury. He then is pulled out of the
           hatch and lowered to the ground.

                   If both the Bradley commander and
           gunner are injured and the turret opening is
           not aligned with the turret shield door, the

 — FM 7-7J                             EFFECTS OF
M-12                          CHEMICAL AGENTS

                   Chemical agents enter the body through
            the eyes, nose, mouth, or skin. Liquid agents
            may contaminate equipment, the ground,
            and foliage. The agent may stay for hours or
            days and be a serious hazard to unprotected
            troops.

                   Chemical agents cannot destroy the
            BFV or its equipment. They can restrict
            equipment use until the equipment is
            sufÏciently decontaminated to reduce the
            hazard. At platoon level, soldiers can
            decontaminate only the mission-essential
            areas (driver’s controls, gunner’s controls,
            and individual weapons). So, all personnel
            must continue to wear protective masks,
            overgarments, overboots, and gloves, once
            chemical contamination has occurred. The
            platoon leader and squad leaders must know
            what their responsibilities are and be
            familiar with the techniques for decontami-
            nation operations. Each company should
            have a specially trained decontamination
            team (AR 220-58) with proper equipment
            (discussed later) to do the job.

                    Liquid chemical agents can restrict the
            use of terrain and buildings. Infantry
            platoons cannot decontaminate terrain. That
            is usually done naturally by the weather.
            Contaminated areas may be either bypassed
            or crossed. They are bypassed whenever
            possible. When crossing is absolutely neces-
            sary, protective equipment is worn. Once
            across the area, soldiers and equipment
            should be decontaminated as soon as the
            situation permits.

                        ALARMS FOR CHEMICAL
                            HAZARD OR ATTACK

                   When a soldier detects a chemical
            hazard, he must immediately stop breathing,
            mask, and give the alarm. The alarm should
            be repeated immediately by every soldier
            after masking.

                                         produces an audible or visual signal when it
                                        detects the presence of chemical agents in the
                                         air. The M43, the detector of the M8 alarm,
                                         will detect nerve, blood, and choking agents.
                                         (The M43A1 only detects nerve agents, but it
                                        detects them at lower concentrations than
                                         does the M43.) It is stowed inside the BFV on
                                        the right rear wall. To detect chemical
                                         agents, the M8 alarm must be removed from
                                        the vehicle, assembled according to
                                        TM 3-6665-225-12, backpacked, or mounted
                                         externally, and placed into operation.

        AFTER A CHEMICAL ATTACK

        Each soldier should remain masked and
continue his mission. He should give any
needed first aid to any casualties in his
immediate vicinity and report the local
casualty status to his next higher leader.
Contaminated skin, clothing, and equipment
should be decontaminated as soon as
possible.

   — FM 7-7J            When planning camouflage and conceal-
N-2             ment, platoons and squads must think about
                the things the enemy will look for, or things
                that will attract his attention to friendly
                positions. These include movement, sha-
               dows, obvious positions, shine or reflected
               light, shape, color, and concentration.

               Movement. Movement attracts attention,
               particularly vehicular movement. Even slight
               movements, such as arm-and-hand signals
               or a soldier walking, may attract the enemy’s
               attention.

               Shadows. Unusual shadows will attract
               attention. Since the BFV is large and has
               a distinct shape, its shadow may be easily
               seen. Hence, every effort should be made to
               break up the vehicle’s outline and cause its
               shadow to blend with shadows cast by
               natural terrain features. Shaded areas
               should be used to the maximum, but shadows
               move as the position of the sun or moon
               changes, and this should be taken into
               account. Vehicles should be repositioned
               accordingly.

               Obvious Positions. Hilltops, road junc-
               tions, and lone buildings should be avoided.
              They may be easily seen by the enemy or
               serve as registration points for enemy
              indirect fire.

              Shine or Reflected Light. In daylight,
              bright or shiny surfaces will reflect sunlight
              and draw the enemy’s attention. At night, an
              exposed light, even one with a red lens, or the
              glow of a cigarette can be seen from far away.

              Shape. The shape of a vehicle or even a
              helmet is easily identified by the enemy.
              Shape and outline of troops and vehicles
              must be broken up by camouflage materials.

              Color. Combat uniforms and even the
              vehicle are colored to blend with wooded
              surroundings. Often, though, colors will not
              blend with the background. For example, if
              the ground is covered with snow, green

                NOISE AND LIGHT                   FM 7-73 —
                        DISCIPLINE                                 N-5

     If a unit does not practice noise and light
discipline at night, the best operational
security measures can be wasted. The most
difÏcult noises to control are noises made by
the vehicle. These also are the most likely
noises to be detected by the enemy. Several
techniques can be used to cut down vehicle

noises.

       When possible, keep night movement toa

minimum because the BFV’s engine and
tracks can be heard at a considerable
distance. Avoid idling engines at extreme
speeds or moving vehicle rapidly and, if
possible, close ramps and hatches before
dark. When closing them after dark, they
should not be slammed shut.

Vehicle light discipline includes:

m Using vision  block  covers       during
    darkness.

w Using the driver's night vision viewer
    (AN/VVS-2).

@ Using night vision goggles.

= Turning off all internal lights.

w Using red filters on flashlights.

a When it is dark and preparations have

    been made, one member of each dis-
    mount team should inspect the
    squad's vehicle from the outside to
    insure that there is no visible light
    being emitted from the vehicle.

     The dismount teams also must practice
noise and light discipline. Noise discipline is
simply avoiding loud noises, such as loud
talking, laughing, or metal-on-metal sounds.
Light discipline involves no smoking or
building fires, and controlling use of flash-

lights.

SECTION III. SIGNAL SECURITY

                                                                         GENERAL

                                                     Signal security (SIGSEC) includes mea-
                                             sures taken to deny or counter enemy
                                             exploitation of electronic emissions. It in-
                                             cludes communications security and elec-
                                             tronic security.

                                                    At the platoon and squad level, SIGSEC
                                             mainly concerns good communication pro-
                                             cedures and electronic counter-countermea-
                                             sures. ECCM are those actions taken to
                                             insure friendly use of the electromagnetic
                                             spectrum against electronic warfare and
                                             includes antijamming, authentication, and
                                             radio discipline. (See Appendix D for com-
                                             munications security details.)

                                                    As far as possible, the radio should be
                                             considered a communications backup. Arm-
                                             and-hand signals, flag signals, whistles,

N-8


---

telephones, flashlight signals, and mes-         ‘FM 7-73 —
sengers are other available means.                                 N-9

      There will be times when the radio must
be used. Platoons and squads should assume
that the enemy is monitoring every radio
transmission and using radio direction
finders to locate transmitting radios. They
also must assume that the enemy under-
stands English and can quickly break
unauthorized codes.

      No matter who is transmitting by
radio, these rules should be followed:

gw Transmit only when necessary.

g Think the message through and know
    exactly what needs to be said before
    keying the transmitter.

a Keep transmissions short, and use call
    signs only as necessary.

# Do not confuse the radio with vehicle

     intercom systems.

m Use proper radiotelephone       proce-
    dures and prowords.

= Operate radios on low power as much
    as possible.

          ENCODED INFORMATION

      In transmissions to the company com-
mander and other platoons, the platoon

leader often will have information that needs
to be encoded. In these situations, the platoon
leader should use the communications-
electronics operating instructions for the
proper encoding procedures and authentica-

tion tables.

      Within the platoon, there seldom is
occasion to send information that requires
code; hence, transmissions are in the clear.
Sensitive information should be passed
orally in a face-to-face meeting of leaders or

sent by messenger.

                  Hasty protective minefields are reported
          to the company commander and recorded on
          DA Form 1355-1-R. The leader puts the
          minefield across likely avenues of approach,
          within range of his organic weapons, and
          covered by the fire of his organic weapons.
          Mines are normally placed on the surface in
          this type of minefield.

          a  HASTY PROTECTIVE

             MINEFIELD

                  The minefield should be recorded before
          the mines are armed. The leader installing
          the minefield should warn adjacent platoons
          and tell the company commander of the
          minefield’s location. When the platoon leaves
          the area (except when forced to withdraw by
          the enemy), it must remove the minefield or
          transfer the responsibility for the minefield
          to the relieving platoon leader.

                 Only metallic mines are used in hasty
          protective minefields. If the mines cannot be

                                                  FM 7-7J—

      When retrieving the mines, the troops
start at the reference point and move to B-1,
using the azimuth and distances as recorded.
They then move from B-1 to the first mine in
row B. However, if B-1 is destroyed, they
move from the reference point to B-2 using
that azimuth and distance. They will now
have to shoot the back azimuth from B-2 to
the last mine. (Add or subtract 180 degrees
from the recorded azimuth.) The stakes at A-
1, B-1, A-2, and B-2 are necessary because it is
safer to find a stake when traversing long
distances than to find a live mine.

or push a hole about the size of a blasting

and .65 centimeter [1/4 inch] in
diameter) in a block of C4 plastic
explosive.

                         STEP 2

                             Cut Fuse

        Cut and discard a 15-centimeter (6-
inch) length from the free end of the time
blasting fuse to prevent a misfire caused
by the exposed powder absorbing mois-
ture from the air.

centimeter (3-foot) section of fuse to

help determine how much fuse is needed

to allow the person detonating the

explosion. Divide this burning time by 3

to find the burning time of 30.5

centimeters (1 foot). Now divide the

time required to allow the person ,

detonating the charge to reach a safe |

distance from the explosion by the burn

time of 30.5 centimeters (1 foot). This y

will give the number of centimeters /

(feet) of fuse needed.                                                  !

              DETONATING CORD
                   FIRING SYSTEM

Methods of Use. Of all the firing systems
for explosives, a detonating cord firing
system is probably the most versatile and in
many cases the most easily installed. It is
especially applicable for underwater and
underground blasting because the blasting
cap of the initiating system may remain
above the water or ground.

      An electric system consisting of an
electric blasting cap, initiated by a blasting

machine or other power source, or a

                                                 0-23


---

—— FM 7-7J

            nonelectric blasting cap initiated by a fuse
            igniter and a length of time blasting fuse, is
            used to initiate detonating cord.

                   The blasting cap, electric or nonelectric,
            is attached to a point 6 inches from the free
            end of the detonating cord by numerous
            wraps of string, wire, cloth, or tape.

            Detonating Cord Connections. A det-
            onating cord clip or square knot pulled tight
            is used to splice the ends of detonating cord.
            At least a 6-inch length should be left free at
            both sides of the knot. When fabric is used to
            cover the detonating cord, the fabric must not
            be removed. The knot may be placed in water
            or in the ground but the cord must be
            detonated from a dry end.

            SQUARE KNOT CONNECTIONS  4

            Branch Line Connections
     A branch line is fastened to a main line

by means ofa clip or a girth hitch with one
extra turn. The angle formed by the branch
line and the cap end of the main line should
not be less than 90 degrees from the direction
from which the blast is coming; at a smaller
angle, the branch line may be blown off the
main line without being detonated. At least6
inches of the running end of the branch lineis

left free beyond the tie.

  a

      A ring main is made by bringing the

 attaching it to itself with a girth hitch with
 one extra turn. This will detonate an almost
 unlimited number of charges. The ring main

                                                                           FM 7-73 —

                Failure of Branch Line

      If the detonating cord main line det-
onates but a branch line fails, fasten a
blasting cap to the branch line and fire it

separately.
        Failure of Charge to Explode

      If the charge is above ground, and the
detonating cord leading to a charge det-
onates but the charge fails to explode, delay
investigation until it is certain that the
charge is not burning. If the charge is in the
ground, wait 30 minutes. If the charge is
intact, insert a new primer. If the charge is
scattered by the detonation of the original
detonating cord, reassemble as much of the
original charge as possible, place a new
charge if necessary, and reprime. Make every
attempt possible to recover all explosives
scattered by misfire, particularly those used
in training exercises.

SECTION III. BREACHING AND CLEARING

                                                                OBSTACLES

                          GENERAL

      Obstacles are used to halt or to slow
 units, or to cause them to move into an area
 selected as a kill zone. If the enemy has
 selected such an area, he will have prepared
 it so that he can inflict great damage on any

 opponent moving into it. The enemy will
 exploit existing obstacles such as defiles,
 rivers, thick woods, swamps, cliffs, canals,

 and built-up areas, and complement them
 with reinforced obstacles. Leaders must
 know the tactics and techniques used to

 overcome reinforced obstacles.
       Some obstacles may not restrict dis-

 mounted elements but will restrict vehicular

                                                                           0-27


---

—FM 7-7J

             movement. The platoon may have to clear
             obstacles to help vehicles go forward.
             Obstacles are normally covered by enemy
             direct and indirect fire to keep attacking
             troops from breaching them. The platoon
             may not be able to keep the enemy from
             knowing that it is going to breach, but it
             should try to keep the enemy from knowing
             where and when it will try to breach.

                                        MINEFIELDS

                    To maintain the momentum of an attack,
             the platoon must be prepared to breach
             minefields.

   TANK DITCHES

      Tank ditches are usually in open terrain.
They are at least 4 meters (13 feet) wide and
1.8 meters (5 feet) deep. The enemy may put
barbed wire and mines in them to keep tank
crews or infantry from dismounting and
using the ditch for shelter. He may prepare
the approaches, sides, and bottom of the
ditch with antitank and antipersonnel mines
or chemicals to make breaching difÏcult.
There are several steps to follow to clear a

tank ditch.
